item.title: KSL Vault: Decades of holiday tradition shine on as Temple Square lights return
item.description:
Temple Square's holiday lights returned Friday after years in which COVID-19 and the square's renovation scaled back or altered the display, a tradition dating to 1965. They will be on through Jan. 1, daily from 6 to 8 a.m. and from 4:30 to 10 p.m.

KSL archive footage shows decades of crowds, including a 1992 visitor who called the moment the lights switch on "magical". In 2011, Eldon Cannon of Temple Square ground services said crews start installing lights in August, with about 75,000 on the Cedar of Lebanon tree alone.

item.title: Ogden woman to spend up to 15 years in prison for physical abuse of her son
item.description:
A judge sentenced Ogden woman Mindy Deanna Murray, 25, to concurrent prison terms of one to 15 years after she pleaded guilty to attempted child torture and two counts of aggravated child abuse involving her young son. Under a plea deal with Weber County prosecutors, the charges were reduced, and Murray admitted seriously injuring the boy between August 2025 and February 2026.

The boy told authorities his mother is "always mean". The plea agreement also says he showed up at his Ogden school with visible facial injuries and that a witness saw Murray hit him an estimated 10 to 12 times in a car.

item.title: Black Friday shoppers undeterred by inflation and bad weather
item.description:
Black Friday shoppers turned out at U.S. stores despite inflation and bad weather that brought flooding, while Adobe reported a record $7.1 billion in online Thanksgiving spending and expects $13 billion to $13.4 billion online on Black Friday. Some mall operators counted more early visitors than last year, including Macerich, up 2% to 4%, and Mall of America, up 8.5% in its first hour.

Adobe said AI-powered shopping doubled the retail-site traffic it drove a year ago. Some shoppers still felt squeezed, including retired veteran Aime Becker of Illinois, who called food prices "astronomical".

item.title: Utah looks at data center guardrails as the national pushback continues
item.description:
Utah lawmakers unveiled a data center framework Nov. 18 that would make developers disclose expected impacts, bar officials from signing nondisclosure agreements and ban evaporative cooling, as proposed projects in Carbon and Juab counties draw local opposition. Rep. Paul Cutler, who presented it, says the goal is to attract committed operators while keeping approval decisions with local communities, though the bill has yet to be fully drafted.

Mona resident Taylor Flake, who said he learned of a nearby data center four months after the county approved it, called the new tools "woefully insufficient." Rep. Kim James, D-Ogden, questioned whether Utah wants data centers at all and called for a "legislative pause".

item.title: Stocks jump to close out an erratic week that was also Wall Street's best in more than a year
item.description:
The S&P 500 rose 1.6% Friday to finish a 5.6% weekly gain, Wall Street's best week since April 2025, after a choppy holiday-shortened stretch led by technology stocks. The rebound came a week after the index closed more than 10% below the record it set last month.

Newly public Anthropic jumped 11% to $91.88, above its $83 IPO price but below its first-day high of $115. Inflation worsened in October, and Brent crude ended near $91 as households began holiday shopping.

item.title: Sandy man federally charged for carjacking 2 vehicles at gunpoint
item.description:
A federal grand jury has indicted Gustavo Dee Chavez, 24, of Sandy, on carjacking and firearm charges, accusing him of pulling a gun on two women in Sandy on Nov. 10 and firing a round into the ground during the first attempt. Chavez, who charges say drove off in the second car before police tracked it by GPS to Saratoga Springs, made his first court appearance Tuesday.

Charges say the first woman handed over her keys but Chavez could not start her SUV, while the second left her keys in the ignition after he threatened to shoot her. Five Saratoga Springs schools briefly went into "secure" status while police took him into custody.

item.title: Ben McAdams is returning to Congress
item.description:
Ben McAdams, who won back his old House seat in this year's Democratic wave, returns to Congress as Utah's lone Democrat and the only member of the state's delegation in the majority. He says that role will help him push Utah priorities such as Great Salt Lake and Colorado River funding, though he expects to clash with the Republican delegation over public lands.

Sen. John Curtis said the pair have had "frank conversations" and predicted public disagreements, but called McAdams someone the delegation can work with. McAdams, who casts himself as a moderate, said he will sometimes break with his own caucus because he puts "solutions above everything else."

item.title: 1 Utah university cracks '40 Beautiful College Campuses' list
item.description:
Utah State University is the only Utah school on U.S. News & World Report's new list of 40 beautiful college campuses, alongside schools such as Harvard, Stanford and Notre Dame. The publication pointed to the Logan campus's setting against Logan Canyon, its historic Old Main building and its status as a certified arboretum.

USU landscape manager Jess Daines, whose crew includes 20 full-time workers and many student employees, credited "many years of hard work". He said the campus has more than 20 tree species and a full-time arborist.

item.title: Army deems lead azide detonation a success but criticism lingers over notification
item.description:
The U.S. Army declared Wednesday's controlled detonation of its aging lead azide stockpile at an Iowa ammunition plant a success, and the EPA says it has detected no airborne lead since. Residents and some elected officials, including Sen. Joni Ernst, have criticized the Army's transparency, and Iowa's governor-elect, Rob Sand, wants an investigation into how the stockpile reached such a precarious point.

Sand said the lead-up "should never have been so chaotic and unclear". Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson countered that residents there had known since a March plant closure, and he believes the Army did its job.

  • Army deems lead azide detonation a success but criticism lingers over notification - ksl.com

item.title: Christmas Celebration brings Santa to Tooele, Grantsville
item.description:
Tooele and Grantsville are holding back-to-back Christmas parades Saturday, starting with Tooele's Magic on Main Street celebration and Santa Parade and ending with Grantsville's lighted floats after dark. Tooele's event opens at 1 p.m. with a market at Veteran's Memorial Park and closes with the mayor lighting the park's tree at 5:30 p.m., and Grantsville's Christmas Light Parade starts at 6 p.m.

Many of the floats move on to Grantsville afterward, where parade-goers get a ticket to an afterparty with Santa and Mrs. Claus at Clark Historic Farm. Tooele County Chamber of Commerce executive director Jared Hamner said the celebration also "brings awareness to small businesses."

item.title: Parowan secures $5M federal grant for economic development
item.description:
Parowan has won a $5 million federal Economic Development Administration grant to build a heavy-haul road, with water, power and fiber lines, out past the Parowan Airport to an industrial park. Mayor Mollie Halterman says the infrastructure should bring businesses and jobs to the Iron County town, which she said had been headed toward becoming a retirement community.

The money came from a disaster-recovery pool, and City Manager Dan Jessen said 2023 flooding in another part of town made Parowan eligible because the development site sits outside the flood zone. Halterman called the money a "huge win" for the city, with a $600,000 state grant and city funds covering the rest of the $6.5 million project.

item.title: More Utahns turning to alternative forms of birth control, research says
item.description:
A new study authored by University of Utah family planning researcher Rebecca Simmons found that use of fertility awareness-based birth control in Utah, Idaho and Nevada nearly doubled, rising from 7.5% in 2022 to 14.5%. Simmons said the regional rate tops the last known national average, and she is calling for more research and better-informed providers, noting the study did not show whether people are using effective methods or unproven ones.

These methods track body signals such as temperature or cycle timing, and Simmons said the rise could also mean more people are struggling to afford standard contraception or get in to see a doctor. "Are people coming to these (methods) because they want to or because they have to?" she asked.

item.title: 'I was willing to try anything': NH mother sets record for living year with pig kidney transplant
item.description:
Molly Falco, 58, of Lyndeborough, New Hampshire, has now lived a full year with a gene-edited pig kidney transplanted at Massachusetts General Hospital, the longest anyone has lived with an organ from another species. She still tires more easily and takes anti-rejection drugs, but hopes the kidney lasts through an expected five-to-seven-year wait for a human donor; otherwise she will have to return to dialysis.

Falco, the fourth person to get such a kidney, had spent nearly a year on dialysis and said she felt no fear: "I practically said yes before doctor really asked the question." Of the three earlier recipients, one died of an unrelated heart problem and two eventually rejected their organs.

item.title: Southern Utah mechanic keeps good times rolling one classic Volkswagen bus at a time
item.description:
Hurricane mechanic Michael Anderson rebuilds classic Volkswagen buses at his one-man shop, DUBFAB, where he said many clients are grandparents who want to take their grandkids out for ice cream. He also upgrades the old buses' suspensions so they can keep pace on today's freeways, and he has a long waiting list.

Anderson owns Utah's "VW" license plate, which he grabbed 15 years ago after finding it available on the DMV website, and keeps it on an unpainted 1963 bus he found in a field in Fredonia, Arizona, in 2018. "There are no bad days when you're driving a Volkswagen bus," he said.

item.title: 3 Utah high schools represent at national marching band competition
item.description:
The American Fork, Green Canyon and Westlake high school marching bands represented Utah at the Bands of America Grand Nationals in Indianapolis Nov. 12-14, where American Fork reached the finals and placed 10th overall. Green Canyon, at its first Grand Nationals, was the last of 30 bands named to the semifinals and finished 26th, third in its division.

Green Canyon director Jacob Andersen said "the kids exploded with energy" when their name came up, and that there were tears. Westlake, back for the first time since 2016, missed the semifinals but called its performance the band's "best run yet".

item.title: New images reveal stadium-size crater left by humanity's first planetary defense test
item.description:
The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has sent back its first images of Dimorphos, the asteroid NASA's DART probe struck in 2022, revealing a stadium-size crater and hundreds of previously unknown boulders around the asteroid pair. In December, Hera is scheduled to close to about 13 kilometers to measure Dimorphos' mass, which team scientist Naomi Murdoch said will show how effective the DART impact was.

Hera team member Sabina Raducan said Dimorphos, which once always showed the same face, is now moving like a "barrel that you throw down the stairs." Murdoch said it is not yet clear whether the boulders are DART debris or have another source, such as the larger asteroid Didymos.

item.title: 'Frosty's Winter Wonderland' is gone, but Salt Lake City honors the 'joy' it brought
item.description:
The Salt Lake City Council voted unanimously last week to award Forrest and Deanna Nunley a certificate of recognition for Frosty's Winter Wonderland, the Avenues hillside Christmas display they ran for more than three decades. The couple announced last month that the display won't return, and they have sold more than 300 of its roughly 500 decorations amid Forrest Nunley's health problems.

Councilman Chris Wharton, whose district includes the Avenues, said the couple "exemplify what it means to invest in a neighborhood and bring people together". Forrest Nunley's only message to the public was to "vote for Santa."

item.title: Utah missionary injured in deadly Brazil bus crash returns to burn unit to give back to patients
item.description:
Mackay Niederhauser, 21, of Davis County, has returned to the University of Utah Hospital burn unit with gift bags for patients spending Thanksgiving there, a year after he spent the holiday in the unit recovering from a bus crash in Brazil. Donations from friends, former teachers, coaches and others paid for blankets, games and $100 DoorDash gift cards meant to help patients enjoy a holiday meal.

Niederhauser was serving a mission for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints when the crash left him with severe friction burns and five weeks in the hospital. He said he hopes a patient opening a basket will "feel loved".

item.title: House Republican leaders tee up major permitting bill in final weeks of majority
item.description:
House Republican leaders plan to bring a bipartisan permitting reform bill that Utah Sen. Mike Lee helped negotiate to a floor vote the week of Nov. 30, sources told the Deseret News, seeking a win before Democrats take over Congress. Passing it by simple majority requires Speaker Mike Johnson to get all his members back for a procedural rule vote, after 21 Republican absences last week pushed the House into an early Thanksgiving recess.

Seven House Democrats who lead tribal and natural resources panels have called the bill "fatally flawed" and urged colleagues to oppose it, while Lee said he is "guardedly optimistic about where things stand." Any changes the House approves would send the bill back to the Senate before President Donald Trump could sign it.

item.title: Discovery of an Egyptian structure hidden for 2,600 years offers clues to ancient engineering
item.description:
Researchers using satellite radar and electrical resistivity tomography have identified a buried mudbrick building from Egypt's 26th dynasty at Buto, an ancient religious and political center in the Nile Delta, according to a study in Acta Geophysica. A sand layer beneath it, which the authors believe was placed on purpose to steady the soft delta ground, could offer clues to ancient foundation engineering.

The building's use is unknown, but the researchers suspect a religious role, possibly a tomb, shrine or priests' residence, and excavations guided by the surveys turned up amulets and an altar. Egyptologist Hussein Bassir, who was not involved, said more investigation is needed to confirm the sand's purpose and that "technology will never replace the archaeologist".


Sources:

  • Discovery of an Egyptian structure hidden for 2,600 years offers clues to ancient engineering - ksl.com

item.title: This woman just ran 7 marathons in 7 days on 7 continents
item.description:
Utah runner Melissa Walker, 50, finished The Great World Race in Miami on Nov. 21, completing seven marathons in seven days on seven continents alongside 76 other runners. After a week of about 26,000 air miles on a chartered plane, Walker said she learned she is a lot tougher than she thought, and she signed up for a Thanksgiving 10K once her husband did.

A snowstorm swapped the planned Antarctica opener for Cape Town, and her finishing times were slower than any of her 27 earlier marathons. She said she hopes others might "do something they think is crazy because I did".

item.title: Small cups, big goal: Salt Lake City students join worldwide record attempt
item.description:
Ensign Elementary students in Salt Lake City stacked plastic cups during the annual worldwide sport-stacking week, Nov. 16-20, joining a global bid to beat the 784,036-participant record set in 2025. Organizers aimed for 800,000 this year, and the verified worldwide count, which can take weeks to tally, will determine whether the record falls.

P.E. teacher Bernadine Winkler, now in her third year entering the school, said she first signed up because one student kept asking for more cup stacking: "I kind of did it for her". She said the activity builds eye-hand coordination and that "any child with any ability can do it".

item.title: Man killed in Salt Lake City shooting after disagreement Wednesday
item.description:
A man was shot and killed late Wednesday outside a Salt Lake City house that police said was serving as an Airbnb, and police arrested 26-year-old Timothy Dewayne Combs. Police said Combs told them that after someone in his group was slapped, he grabbed a gun from a Tesla as the man approached and began assaulting him, then shot the man at close range.

Witnesses at a neighboring house told police the man had walked over to talk with people near the Tesla before several men got out of the car and at least one fired. A second detained person backed Combs' account, describing a "struggle for a gun".

  • Man killed in Salt Lake City shooting after disagreement Wednesday - ksl.com

item.title: Social media firms not liable for the 2022 Buffalo mass shooting, New York's top court says
item.description:
New York's Court of Appeals ruled 4-3 on Monday that Meta, Alphabet and Reddit are not liable for the 2022 racist attack at a Buffalo supermarket, keeping lawsuits from survivors and victims' relatives dismissed. Matthew Bergman, a lawyer for the family of victim Heyward Patterson, said they are weighing their legal options.

The majority found the suits did not show the killings were a "natural and foreseeable consequence" of how the companies built and ran their platforms. Three dissenting judges, in an opinion by Judge Jenny Rivera, said the plaintiffs had made a strong enough case to proceed.

  • Social media firms not liable for the 2022 Buffalo mass shooting, New York's top court says - ksl.com

item.title: As plans for a Carbon County data center and nuclear reactors advance, residents push to be heard
item.description:
Carbon County residents asked Utah's Trust Lands Administration board on Thursday to revisit the lease it approved two months ago for Valar Atomics, a California company planning a data center and hundreds of small nuclear reactors in the county. The agency said later that day it would not reopen the deal, calling the signed lease a legally binding contract.

Elizabeth Trostle, who lives near Wellington, said she only heard about the project weeks after the board took up the proposal and asked why residents had to "learn about something of this magnitude through NPR". Valar has also applied to the Bureau of Land Management for land in the same area, a request the federal agency is in the early stages of reviewing.

item.title: 22 states are suing the feds for ending immigrant housing aid
item.description:
Twenty-two state attorneys general, in a suit led by New York, California and Massachusetts, are challenging a HUD rule that would end federal housing aid for households that include ineligible noncitizens, arguing it breaks federal law. Unless a court blocks it, the rule takes effect Dec. 14, and a Salt Lake City Housing Authority official says about a dozen local families would lose their housing.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner says the rule "ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars." The states counter that the law protects mixed-status families already receiving prorated aid; HUD's own impact analysis puts the rule's potential cost at up to $251 million.

item.title: Santa Claus getting new 'mid-century' sleigh in time for Ogden's Holiday Electric Light Parade
item.description:
Ogden's Santa sleigh float will roll out a mid-century makeover at Saturday's Holiday Electric Light Parade, after David Andora and Sean Hunt of Tru-Tone rebuilt it over the summer as a volunteer project for the city. The parade starts at 5:30 and leads into the season's Christmas Village lighting on the Ogden Municipal Building grounds.

Once gold and lying in a huddle, the fiberglass reindeer now fly from posts on a float lit by a few thousand of the company's bulbs, replacing a glittery look Andora said resembled "a '90s shopping mall." Ogden cultural services director Ashley Bockwoldt said "the finished sleigh has truly blown me away".

item.title: Supreme Court to hear case over prayer gatherings in a private home
item.description:
The U.S. Supreme Court will hear arguments Dec. 9 on whether Daniel Grand, who alleges University Heights, Ohio, officials chilled his Orthodox Jewish prayer gatherings at home, can sue in federal court even though the city never made a final permit decision. A ruling for Grand could let people with similar claims argue they need not finish a local zoning process before suing, though his move out of the city, which he reported to the court in September, has raised a question about whether the case can go forward.

In a video posted by Alliance Defending Freedom, which represents him, Grand said his garbage stopped being collected and his property taxes went up, "just mine". The group's CEO, Kristen Waggoner, posted that "No one needs a permit to pray".

item.title: Ballet West Academy director releases worship album arranged for ballet class
item.description:
Evelyn Cisneros-Legate, director of Ballet West Academy in Salt Lake City and a former San Francisco Ballet prima ballerina, has released a 27-track album of contemporary Christian songs arranged as solo piano music for a full ballet class. The album, performed by pianist Sid Fendley, is out now on streaming services and in physical copies, and she and her husband have already started a song list for a second one.

Each arrangement was built around the tempo and phrasing of a specific barre or center exercise, and Cisneros-Legate said students at the academy were more engaged than ever when she used it. She said that with the album, "pliés and pirouettes can be turned into praise."

item.title: Harvest Arts Market supports vendors while preparing community members for the holidays
item.description:
More than 32 Native American art and craft vendors sold their work at the Urban Indian Center of Salt Lake's Harvest Arts Market over the weekend, an annual event held there for over 25 years. Outreach manager Rhonda Honey DuVall said the market lets Indigenous entrepreneurs earn extra holiday income beyond their regular jobs.

Vendor Anthony Martinez, who makes ribbon skirts, jewelry and leather goods with his wife and sister, said the event feels like "a big family reunion". The center, in Salt Lake City since 1974, also runs clinics in West Valley City and Murray.

item.title: 10 years later, fallen Utah Highway Patrol trooper's memory lives on
item.description:
Ten years after Utah Highway Patrol trooper Eric Ellsworth died after a car hit him while he was managing traffic at a low-hanging power line in Garland, his widow, Janica Ellsworth, says she has tried to keep her promise to move forward while raising their three sons. A 20-foot white cross that an anonymous family erected beside I-15 in Box Elder County in 2017 still introduces some passing drivers to a man they never knew.

"I think you just get more used to carrying that grief," Janica Ellsworth said, adding that she sometimes catches her late husband in the boys' mannerisms. She said strangers have reached out after googling his name, and she called the cross "such a beautiful tribute to him."

item.title: Utah teen's dream of marching in Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade delayed by historic postponement
item.description:
Alex Harris, an 18-year-old from Lake Point in Tooele County, traveled to New York to help handle the Spider-Man balloon in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, only for organizers to postpone the parade until Saturday. Harris and his family rebooked flights and added a hotel night so he can still march and his parents can watch in person.

Harris, who spent months training on balloon pilots' hand signals, said there were "a couple of tears" when he got the news, but he sees an upside. "Not only are we making history with our 100th parade, we are also making history with not marching on Thanksgiving Day," he said.

item.title: Seasonal depression can affect mood, energy and motivation during winter months
item.description:
Shorter, colder winter days can bring on seasonal affective disorder, a recurring depression that can affect mood, energy and motivation, and licensed counselor Daniel Allen of Creekside Counseling says holiday pressures can compound it. Allen recommends making time for people and favorite activities, getting outside, and paying attention to sleep, hydration, nutrition and exercise.

Allen says the condition doesn't always look like sadness and can surface as anxiety, irritability, a racing mind or trouble sleeping. Describing the season, Allen said "our biology slows down, but our life doesn't slow down."

item.title: Weber County accord with ICE to crack down on illegal immigration draws fire; sheriff defends it
item.description:
Most of the more than 20 people who addressed Weber County commissioners Tuesday criticized the sheriff's office's 287(g) agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and Commissioner Gage Froerer said the commission would examine the policy over the next two to three weeks. Sheriff Ryan Arbon, who did not attend, defended the accord Wednesday, arguing that law enforcement can't pick which laws to enforce.

Critics pointed to a Chilean couple with no criminal records who were detained for overstaying their visas after a traffic stop, and Democrat C.J. Hernandez, newly elected to the Utah Senate, said the agreement is causing "a lot of stress and fear" in the community. Arbon said two deputies work under the agreement and contact ICE only when they come across people suspected of being in the country illegally during routine duties.

item.title: Feel the need to 'fix' your brain? Cognition researchers say this fix can help
item.description:
A study coauthored by University of Utah medical researcher Ka-Ho Wong found that self-reported trouble concentrating, remembering and making decisions doubled over 10 years among adults ages 18 to 39. University of Utah cognition researcher Brennan Payne says reading full books exercises the brain in ways short screen text does not and may build reserve that protects cognitive health later in life.

Wong said the team expected older adults to drive the increase, but "we saw the drive was actually from the younger population". Sharon LaFleur, who joined a Bookish SLC reading party at a downtown pub, suspects her phone is the culprit, calling it a "little flashlight of death" that has kind of taken over her evenings.

item.title: Why Utah's Hogle Zoo is adding a $40 parking fee — for a few days
item.description:
Utah's Hogle Zoo will charge $40 to park in its lot from Dec. 2 through Dec. 5, while the Christkindlmarkt across the street at This Is The Place Heritage Park draws large crowds. Members and guests holding prepaid daytime admission or Hogle Holidays tickets are exempt, and others can put the fee toward tickets or paid experiences inside the zoo.

The market, held since 2012, now draws more than 140,000 visitors a year, and organizers' free offsite shuttle parking hasn't stopped the impact on the zoo. Zoo officials said it creates parking demand "beyond our control," and normal parking rules resume Dec. 6.

item.title: How a little cookie is helping a historic inn near the Grand Canyon through tough times
item.description:
The family that owns Jacob Lake Inn near the Grand Canyon's North Rim says its homemade cookies have kept customers coming after wildfires and flooding cut into visits, including the blaze that destroyed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge. Owner Melinda Rich Marshall says the inn lost about $1.5 million last year, and the family is lobbying Congress for help for gateway communities.

The bakery began in 1975 despite doubts anyone would pay for homemade cookies, and by 2024 Marshall estimates it was turning out about 1,500 a day; it now offers 17 varieties in the busy season. "People are still coming for the cookies, and we're really, really grateful for that," Marshall said.

item.title: Millcreek appoints new city councilman to fill seat left by state senator-elect
item.description:
Millcreek has picked planning commissioner Jacob Richardson to fill the District 1 City Council seat Sylvia Catten is leaving after winning election to the Utah Senate. Richardson will be sworn in Jan. 11, 2027, and serve until Catten's term ends in early 2028, with the seat on next year's municipal ballot.

Catten, a Democrat who has been on the council since the city incorporated in 2016, will replace Sen. Nate Blouin in Senate District 13 in January. Richardson, a senior policy adviser at Western Resource Advocates, said in a statement that he believes in "collaborative, resident-informed governance" that supports city staff and engages residents.

item.title: Thanksgiving food prices drop in Utah despite national upward trend
item.description:
The American Farm Bureau Federation's annual survey puts a traditional Thanksgiving dinner for 10 in Utah at $51.19 this year, 8% below 2025, even as the national average rose to $58.63. Turkey drove Utah's drop, with its price down 22% in the state while climbing 10% nationwide.

Utah Farm Bureau vice president Tyson Roberts said, "It's nice to see a drop for once." Nancy Biele, a Minneapolis visitor shopping at a Salt Lake City Macey's, still described food prices as "Very expensive" but said the holiday is a time people are willing to spend more.

item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: As GLP-1 use grows, patients and doctors rethink Thanksgiving dinner
item.description:
As more Americans take GLP-1 weight loss drugs, the medications could be changing how some Americans approach Thanksgiving by shrinking appetites and portions, with a Gallup poll finding 11% of U.S. adults currently use them for weight loss. Doctors say people new to the drugs should watch for side effects, and Louisville gastroenterologist John Horlander advises moderation and smaller portions.

Raleigh wellness coach Kim Dillard Davis, who has lost about 80 pounds since 2023 and whose family now celebrates at restaurants, urged relatives not to question how little she eats: "Let us eat small portions and be happy". University of Michigan psychologist Ashley Gearhardt, who cautioned guests against policing others' plates, said there may be "fewer turkey comas at the end of the day".

  • As GLP-1 use grows, patients and doctors rethink Thanksgiving dinner - ksl.com

item.title: Salt Lake City considers 'discounted' lease for homeless village to quadruple land size
item.description:
Salt Lake City is weighing whether to let The Other Side Village, a community for people who were chronically homeless, grow from 8.1 to 37.5 acres of city land under another below-market lease, which would take it from 60 homes to 420. The City Council has set a public hearing for Dec. 1, with a vote tentatively planned for Dec. 8.

The proposed term sheet has the city collecting $2 a year through at least October 2063, with at least 324 units reserved for people who meet HUD's definition of "chronically homeless and homeless". City community and neighborhood officials told the council a below-market ground lease is "an appropriate use of City resources," while the academy that owns the village drew scrutiny in June over its strict treatment rules.

item.title: Rescue Mission serves hundreds of Thanksgiving meals to homeless Utahns
item.description:
The Rescue Mission of Salt Lake held its annual Thanksgiving banquet Wednesday, with Gov. Spencer Cox and first lady Abby Cox among the volunteers serving meals to hundreds of Utahns in need as the mission also offered clothes, haircuts and showers. Counting leftovers delivered to people living on the street, the mission estimates it fed more than 1,000 people.

Speaking to the banquet's love-thy-neighbor theme, the governor said Jesus taught that "everyone is our neighbor, especially those who are different than us." Donnie Spears, who has spent several months in a shelter with her 3-year-old son, is hoping to find a home by Christmas.

item.title: Judge declines to issue a ban on taxpayer-funded, pro-Trump ads critics called propaganda
item.description:
U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan on Wednesday declined to extend a temporary block on the Trump administration's taxpayer-funded ads, ruling the Democratic National Committee hadn't shown it was likely to win its claim that they were illegal propaganda. Her earlier order had blocked some of the ads through Nov. 25, and a judge in a similar New York case also turned down a long-term ban.

With the midterms over, AliKhan rejected the DNC's argument that the ads could still cause harm in December runoffs or the 2028 race, writing that "the court is unpersuaded" at this stage. A DNC spokesperson said the party was "disappointed" and vowed to keep fighting.

item.dc:creator: Ali Swenson and Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press

item.title: Utah Giving Machine kiosks help fund small businesses worldwide
item.description:
Donations made at Utah's Giving Machine kiosks are funding Mentors International, a nonprofit that gives entrepreneurs in developing countries business training and a 10-month mentorship. Gifts such as chickens and business kits help families start or expand small businesses.

Emmanuella Gyamfi, the nonprofit's director in Ghana, said the donations are "creating a ripple effect for families as well as people with disabilities and even primarily women". Board member Liz Mumford said pairing a gift with mentoring turns it into "something that creates continual change" for families.

item.title: UVU Culinary Arts Institute feeds 'elite and gourmet' Thanksgiving meals to nearly 400
item.description:
Faculty from the Utah Valley University Culinary Arts Institute cooked a Thanksgiving dinner for people in need Tuesday at Salt Lake County's Central City Recreation Center that drew more than 370 people, the biggest turnout in the event's 31 years. Organizers said guests can often take home a second plate, helping stretch the meal into the next day for people facing food insecurity.

Chef Troy Wilson, who chairs the institute, said all seven full-time faculty pitched in and that 150 pounds of potatoes were peeled the day before, while beginning baking students made 55 pies. County organizer Lauren Brady suggested the food's quality helped draw the crowd: "It is elite and gourmet."

item.title: Utah awards $9.3M to local agricultural producers, food business to strengthen food supply
item.description:
The Utah Department of Food and Agriculture has awarded $9.3 million to 41 farms, ranches and food processors to improve processing, storage and distribution of local food, the first round of up to $50 million expected over five years from federal Rural Health Transformation money. The next round of applications opens in January 2027 and closes Feb. 28.

The department says every funded project gets at least 70% of its inputs from Utah, 28 are expected to help tribal communities get food, and 32 will help connect producers with schools and other institutions. Commissioner Kelly Pehrson said the goal is "helping more Utah-produced food reach Utah families."

item.title: Man killed by South Jordan police shot at officers first, police say
item.description:
South Jordan police say Anthony Wallace Weber, 31, fired through a door at officers before two of them shot and killed him early Tuesday during a SWAT response to a report that he was threatening a 22-year-old woman with a gun and not letting her leave. The officers are on standard administrative leave while the Unified Police Department conducts an independent investigation.

According to police, the call came from the woman's mother, and officers who reached the woman behind a barricaded bedroom door say Weber grabbed the muzzle of an officer's gun before they fired. State court records show Weber had prior convictions for aggravated assault and stalking involving a former girlfriend and was paroled in July; police have not said whether the woman Tuesday is that same person.


Sources:

  • Man killed by South Jordan police shot at officers first, police say - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Man accused of shooting out rear window of car that drove around him
item.description:
A 40-year-old West Valley man, Elijah Manuel Martinez, has been charged with aggravated assault and firearm discharge with road rage enhancements after prosecutors say he fired a handgun through the rear window of a Kia whose driver had pulled around his truck at a red light. Prosecutors asked a judge to keep him jailed in Salt Lake County without bail pending trial.

Charging documents say a passenger in the Kia filmed the truck's license plate, letting West Valley police find and stop Martinez, and that the bullet lodged in the back seat. Prosecutors called the Nov. 19 shooting an "overreaction to a person driving around his vehicle" and said it shows he is a danger to the community.

  • Man accused of shooting out rear window of car that drove around him - ksl.com

item.title: Army calls detonation of bomb chemicals in Iowa a success after earlier fears of a toxic plume
item.description:
The U.S. Army detonated its entire 5-ton stockpile of degraded lead azide at the Army's Iowa ammunition plant in Middletown on Wednesday, and the Army said early signs showed no toxic dust reached nearby homes and farms. Government agencies still plan more testing in the coming weeks, and independent researchers intend to test water sources, farms, homes and playgrounds.

Plant staff found in March that the chemical had partly crystallized and could go off on its own in cold weather, and court documents show the Army moved the date three times amid public backlash. Bystander Tim Brandt of Burlington told the AP, "It seemed like government put fear in a lot of people over nothing", while nearby resident Lucy Giehl said, "I don't think lead danger goes away any time soon".

item.title: As US pushes to 'win' AI race, politicians and groups call for regulation
item.description:
Former Utah Sen. Mitt Romney, a University of Utah communication professor and the advocacy group Utah Civic Compact are among those pressing for AI regulation as the U.S. pushes to win the technology race. In a Tuesday post on X, Romney faulted the U.S. for rushing AI ahead without safeguards to beat China while also selling China the chips it needs.

Professor Isabelle Freiling said the public needs a say, arguing that "you would not let Exxon decide how to regulate" oil. Clark Dice of Utah Civic Compact told KSL that "AI should not be making decisions that humans would otherwise be held accountable for" and that the public should be involved.

item.title: Couple credits Donny Osmond with saving their house after smoker fire
item.description:
Donny Osmond hosed down a burning backyard smoker at the South Jordan home of Debbie and Tim Hong on Sunday, the couple says, after a neighbor knocked to warn them their house was on fire. Tim Hong believes grease dripped into a bucket under the Traeger and melted a nearby shop vac, though he says he had switched the smoker off.

Unified Fire's Nate Cochran advises keeping smokers at least 10 feet from any structure and calling 911 first if a fire starts. Debbie Hong thanked the entertainer "for saving our house, and maybe our lives".

  • Couple credits Donny Osmond with saving their house after smoker fire - ksl.com

item.title: Federal jury finds Idaho man guilty of COVID-19 fraud, laundering over $195K in relief funding
item.description:
A federal jury on Nov. 19 convicted Pocatello resident Christopher Curtis of bank and wire fraud plus three money-laundering counts involving more than $195,000 in COVID-19 relief funds. Curtis is set to be sentenced Feb. 11, 2027, with a possible maximum of 110 years in prison and a $1.5 million fine.

Besides a $93,900 Economic Impact Disaster Loan for a business that existed only on paper, Curtis obtained a $101,667.67 Paycheck Protection Program loan for Preferred Nevada Logistics by claiming four employees who did not exist. He spent the PPP money on personal costs and stock trades that lost $160,000.

item.title: Consumer confidence soars with elections in the rearview mirror and gas prices in retreat
item.description:
The Conference Board's consumer confidence index jumped to 103.3 in November from 91.9 in October, as gas prices kept falling and election uncertainty faded. The rise could bode well for holiday retailers, though economists say such surveys have become weaker predictors of spending.

Confidence rose sharply among Democrats and independents but slipped modestly among Republicans. Conference Board senior economist Fergus McCormick said that while consumers still voiced frustration with high costs, "some comments cited hope for the general economy."


Sources:

  • Consumer confidence soars with elections in the rearview mirror and gas prices in retreat - ksl.com

item.title: How to spot holiday shopping and charity scams
item.description:
AARP fraud prevention director Kathy Stokes is urging holiday shoppers to look into unfamiliar online sellers before handing over money. Paying by credit card lets buyers dispute a charge for an item that never arrives, a protection Stokes said peer-to-peer payment apps aren't obligated to offer.

Reports to the Federal Trade Commission put last year's losses from scams that started on social media at more than $2 billion, and shopping scams topped the list. Stokes suggested searching a company's name along with "scam or fraud" before buying.

  • How to spot holiday shopping and charity scams - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt, KSL

item.title: After back-to-back floods, one neighbor's nonprofit helps Hurricane rebuild
item.description:
La Verkin resident Cherie Santiago has formed a nonprofit, Routes and Roots, to help Hurricane neighbors rebuild after floods in August and again on Oct. 22 damaged their homes. The IRS approved its 501(c)(3) status three days before the second flood, and Santiago has since raised another $20,000 for relief.

Donations routed through an existing nonprofit after the first flood raised $200,000 for repairs, only for the second storm to wipe out that work. Santiago hopes the group can build a base so "we're not starting off at square one" if disaster strikes again.

item.title: An unclassified CIA system was breached in a cyberattack, AP source says
item.description:
An unclassified CIA system that handles open-source intelligence was breached in a cyberattack, a person familiar with the incident told The Associated Press. The source said no classified information was involved and the issue has been resolved.

The FBI is separately investigating an apparent hack of a law enforcement database it maintains, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has blamed a recent string of outages largely on hurried patches and upgrades meant to keep pace with hackers armed with sophisticated AI tools. Which information was compromised in the CIA breach, and who was responsible, remains unclear.

item.title: Curtis questions Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO
item.description:
Utah Sen. John Curtis questioned Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, asking which U.S. officials told the board his return posed no national security risk. Curtis, a Republican, said Huang was right to leave after the affair became public and noted the board brought him back while its independent investigation was still underway.

Huang had stepped down after his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, came to light. Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton called for a congressional probe, writing that the controversy is "just the tip of the iceberg".

  • Curtis questions Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO - ksl.com

item.title: Health officials, food experts give tips for safe food handling as Thanksgiving approaches
item.description:
Salt Lake County Health Department food protection supervisor Andrea Gamble is urging Thanksgiving cooks to skip washing the turkey and to confirm with a food thermometer that it reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit. Gamble said leftovers keep three or four days in the refrigerator and should be reheated to the same temperature.

Gamble also warned that "Pop-up timers are no substitute for a thermometer." Anyone sickened by a meal can report it at IGotSick.Health.Utah.gov.


Sources:

item.title: Tech outages are piling up, and AI is raising the stakes. Could this be the new normal?
item.description:
A run of outages this month at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, Apple, the FAA and the NSA, along with a reported breach of an unclassified CIA system, has some fearing that such disruptions could become the new normal. The government and the companies say there is no evidence the outages are linked or caused by an attack, though AI tools are raising the stakes for internet security.

After AI helped expose widespread PHP vulnerabilities, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said patching that followed the alert caused some NSA systems to "not come back up" as expected. Sen. Mark Warner said the disruptions "should serve as a wake-up call."

  • Tech outages are piling up, and AI is raising the stakes. Could this be the new normal? - ksl.com

item.title: From Black Friday to safety concerns with gifts for kid, Primary Children's expert urges parents to act fast
item.description:
Trauma coordinator Katherine Stokes is warning parents that a button battery that gets stuck in a young child's esophagus can cause burns and that standard bike helmets may not protect kids riding e-bikes. Stokes said a suspected lodged battery calls for 911 or an immediate emergency room trip, and she recommended helmets certified to the NTA 8776 e-bike standard.

Regular bike helmets are crash-tested to 14 mph, Stokes said, while the e-bike helmet she demonstrated is tested to 28 mph. "On these e-bikes, it's not enough," she said.

item.title: Box Elder County sheriff appears in court in automobile homicide case
item.description:
Box Elder County Sheriff Kevin Potter, charged with automobile homicide in the death of 22-year-old motorcyclist Katie Sue Ruth Huggins, made a brief first court appearance by video Tuesday. Potter is being held in the Weber County Jail while on paid leave, and the case is next set for Dec. 1.

Charging papers say a blood test two hours after the Oct. 27 Ogden crash put Potter's blood-alcohol level at 0.065, above Utah's 0.05 limit. Defense attorney Cara Tangaro said she would likely seek a separate hearing on bail.

  • Box Elder County sheriff appears in court in automobile homicide case - ksl.com

item.title: Longtime Utah high school sports official Jeff Cluff on life support after stroke
item.description:
Jeff Cluff, 49, an associate director of the Utah High School Activities Association, is on life support in a St. George hospital after a stroke and surgery to remove a blood clot that later returned. His family plans to let him pass peacefully once testing for organ donation is complete, according to a post from his daughter.

Cluff, who joined the association in 2014 and umpired Division I college baseball, often spoke up about officials leaving because of poor behavior by fans, coaches and especially parents. His mother, Carol Cluff, said, "He loved people."

item.title: 2 men arrested over suspected burglary at Prince William and Kate's country home
item.description:
Norfolk police arrested two men on suspicion of burglary and trespassing after a reported break-in Monday evening at Prince William and Princess Catherine's home on the Sandringham estate. The men were still in custody without charges Tuesday, and police said nobody was in the property at the time.

The Sun reported that masked men got into the house, Anmer Hall. Kensington Palace said it would not comment on security matters.

item.title: Temple Square fully reopens for Christmas season
item.description:
With construction finished, Temple Square in Salt Lake City is fully open for the Christmas season for the first time in seven years. Its lights switch on Friday at 4:30 p.m. and will glow nightly through New Year's Day, including displays closer to the Salt Lake Temple than ever.

A light tunnel made of cards from people around the world sharing feelings about Jesus Christ and Christmas debuts this year, and the historic cedar of Lebanon tree will be lit for the first time since construction began. "This year, everything will be open," said Jay Warnick, Temple Square's ground services manager.

  • Temple Square fully reopens for Christmas season - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Raise the Future brings adoptive families together at Boondocks
item.description:
Raise the Future gathered adoptive and guardianship families at Boondocks in Draper for its annual National Adoption Month outing. The group's Rachel Waddell said meeting others who understand the trauma and loss behind adoption can make a meaningful difference.

Misty Robinson, who with her husband became guardian of two granddaughters, credits the group's classes and in-home support, saying the family now has "so much hope and more joy, less chaos in our home." Hazel, one of two sisters at the outing with the grandparents raising them, said of their grandmother, "She makes us feel safe and happy."

item.title: Full extent of Christa Pike injuries 'still unknown' 2 months after her botched execution, her attorney says in legal filing
item.description:
Christa Pike's attorney asked a Nashville court Monday to make Tennessee's corrections department allow two psychologists retained by the defense to examine her, saying the full extent of her injuries from the failed Sept. 30 execution is still unknown. The team has requested an emergency hearing, while a corrections lawyer wrote in an email that such visits would amount to prohibited ongoing treatment.

Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital and has since regained the ability to talk and walk with help, while Gov. Bill Lee has said he is not inclined to commute her sentence. In a statement last month, Pike said, "healing is not the same as being okay."

item.title: Houthi rebels close in on Aden as Yemeni forces dig in behind a fortified line
item.description:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels have advanced to about 40 miles from Aden, the southern city that houses Yemen's internationally recognized government, a Yemeni military official said Tuesday. Army spokesman Col. Majed al-Nuzaily said troops pulled back from the western coast now hold a defensive line north and west of the city.

Al-Nuzaily called Aden "a red line" and recalled that its residents drove the Houthis out in 2015. Elsewhere in the region, Iran said three oil tankers caught fire after striking mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and Gaza officials reported at least nine Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes.

item.title: Chinese tech giant Huawei is guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, US jury finds
item.description:
A federal jury in New York convicted Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiring to steal trade secrets and of bank fraud, but acquitted the Chinese company of racketeering conspiracy, the most serious charge. Huawei could face billions of dollars in penalties, and its lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal.

Court records list Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions and T-Mobile among the companies prosecutors said were victimized. Heberlig, who noted that much of the allegedly stolen material was already public, said: "You can't steal a secret that isn't a secret".

item.title: A UK site ranked US ski resorts on popularity. Here's how Utah fared
item.description:
Snowbird and Deer Valley placed fourth and sixth in a popularity ranking of U.S. ski resorts from UK travel site Holidu, which put half of Utah's 16 resorts in its top 50 for the 2026-27 season. The search-data ranking lands as Brighton, Alta, Park City Mountain and Snowbird open ahead of Thanksgiving after storms left Alta and Brighton with nearly 4 feet of snow.

Washington's Crystal Mountain topped the national list with more than 100,000 average monthly searches. Ski Utah president and CEO Nathan Rafferty said earlier this month that last year's poor season created "pent-up demand" for this one.

item.title: Trump grants Thanksgiving pardons for turkeys Freedom and Feathers at the White House
item.description:
President Donald Trump pardoned two West Virginia turkeys, Freedom and Feathers, at a White House ceremony Tuesday, though only Freedom appeared on the South Lawn after a public online vote. Both birds will spend the rest of their lives at Texas A&M University.

Trump said the ceremony will move next year to the White House ballroom now being built, and he voiced bafflement at Democrats' midterm gains, saying, "I don't know what the hell happened with this last election."

item.title: Navajo Nation man given 16 years in prison for fatal shooting
item.description:
A federal judge sentenced Chevel Cottonwood, a 35-year-old Navajo Nation member, to 16 years in prison for the June 2025 shooting death of Winston Billie in San Juan County. Cottonwood had pleaded guilty in August to voluntary manslaughter and to a felon-in-possession gun count, and will serve three years of probation after release.

U.S. District Judge Ann Marie McIff Allen set 13 years for the manslaughter count and three more for the gun charge. In the plea, Cottonwood said he killed Billie "upon sudden quarrel or heat of passion."

item.title: Trump gives Medal of Freedom to Giuliani, a fierce political ally who led New York through 9/11
item.description:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday gave former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Medal of Freedom, the country's top civilian award. Giuliani, 82, was hailed for leading the city after the Sept. 11 attacks, though courts later disbarred him in New York and Washington over false statements about the 2020 election.

In a statement, Giuliani said he shares the credit with those who "worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me" and especially those who died in their shared causes. His son, Andrew Giuliani, said his father's work over the past six years would be remembered as "one of the most important legal jobs" ever done by an attorney.

item.title: House payments down again in the US, at least for now
item.description:
Redfin data shows the typical U.S. monthly mortgage payment slipped about $37 to $2,723 as of Nov. 15, near a two-month low but still 8.2% above a year ago. Redfin notes the relief may not last, since the figure assumes a 7.11% rate; Freddie Mac's 30-year average rose to 7.28% the following week.

The median sale price, $388,516, was down 0.4% from a year earlier, and Austin, Texas, posted the steepest drop among the 50 largest metros, none of which is in Utah, at 10%. San Francisco led price gains with a 14.1% jump.

item.title: Thanksgiving travel could create road delays up to 40 minutes in Utah, UDOT warns
item.description:
UDOT engineers project Thanksgiving traffic could add 30 to 40 minutes to Sunday drives north on I-15, both between St. George and Cedar City and between Nephi and Spanish Fork. Wednesday's southbound rush from Spanish Fork to Nephi could add up to 25 minutes, with the worst likely around 2 p.m.

AAA projects about 85% of the roughly 81.5 million Americans traveling for the holiday will go by car. AAA Mountain West spokesman David Caltabiano said that despite high gas prices, "they will still drive to see their loved ones."

  • Thanksgiving travel could create road delays up to 40 minutes in Utah, UDOT warns - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Pope Francis' private diary describes a profound spiritual crisis and encounters with the devil
item.description:
The Vatican on Tuesday published excerpts from Pope Francis' private diary describing a deep spiritual crisis in 2021-22 and what he experienced as encounters with the devil. Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, who curated the book, ties the crisis to a temptation toward omnipotent power, and by the end of 2022 Francis had apparently come through the crisis by trusting in God.

Reflecting on the 2018 Chile abuse scandal, Francis wrote that he "saw the entrance to hell." The entries span 1992 to Aug. 18, 2024, though Fernández says the pope kept his most confidential thoughts in an unreadable code that the book leaves out.


Sources:

  • Pope Francis' private diary describes a profound spiritual crisis and encounters with the devil - ksl.com

item.title: Utah AG moves to dismiss charges against Kalshi after it blocks service in state
item.description:
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown's office has moved to dismiss criminal gambling charges against prediction market Kalshi after the company cut off access to its platform in Utah on Monday. The motion seeks dismissal without prejudice, meaning the charges could be refiled later.

Kalshi contends Utah has no authority to regulate it, and spokeswoman Jacki McGavick called the pause "an unfortunate outcome" for more than 177,000 Utah users. Brown said Tuesday, "Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges."


Sources:

item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Utah law letting immigrant university students pay lower in-state tuition could be targeted again
item.description:
Utah and the U.S. Department of Justice have asked a federal judge to pause the DOJ lawsuit targeting a state law allowing immigrants in the country illegally to pay in-state tuition, noting a bill file is open to amend or repeal the program in the 2027 session. If Judge Dustin B. Pead agrees, the stay would run until Jan. 29, when both sides would update the court.

Two bills aimed at the tuition provision stalled last year. Utah Senate deputy chief of staff Aundrea Peterson said the matter "will be an item the Senate will likely review over the coming months".

item.title: Provo food bank closure leaves gaps as community steps up to help
item.description:
The closure of Provo's Community Action Services and Food Bank has cut off regular deliveries to many of Alpine School District's 15 school food pantries heading into Thanksgiving. Tabitha's Way, which previously didn't serve Orem, will now open to Orem families and helped district staff assemble 1,167 holiday meals, 500 of them for district families.

Orem Junior High pantry coordinator Sandi Nelson said "families don't know where they can go and get food," and that the pantry lacks fresh produce, milk and eggs. District leaders said the school pantries still need donations to stay stocked in the coming weeks.


Sources:

  • Provo food bank closure leaves gaps as community steps up to help - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Immigrant detained in Provo for allegedly distributing stickers with messages targeting Trump
item.description:
Federal agents arrested Venezuelan immigrant Hector Alejandro Mujica-Hernandez in Provo in October over stickers he allegedly handed out urging people to shoot President Donald Trump, the Department of Homeland Security said Monday. He was being held at an ICE detention center in Louisiana as of Monday, and online federal court records showed no criminal charges against him.

DHS says he entered the country legally in 2016 and overstayed his visa, and Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the department "will not tolerate death threats of any kind." A GoFundMe linked from the Instagram page of People of Provo Against ICE, the group at whose meeting DHS says the stickers were distributed, calls him "a pillar to our community" and seeks help with his legal costs.


Sources:

  • Immigrant detained in Provo for allegedly distributing stickers with messages targeting Trump - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Rivals unite to support Mountain Ridge basketball star battling cancer
item.description:
Varsity players from six rival high schools gathered at Mountain Ridge High in Herriman on Monday for a three-point shooting contest to raise money for Sentinels guard Spencer Perry, 18, who has Hodgkin lymphoma. Perry plans to keep playing as much as he can, starting with Tuesday night's game, before chemotherapy begins Dec. 7.

Teams sank 200 shots, each one adding to the fund for Perry's family. Doctors have offered encouraging news, and Perry said, "It's not super scary because it's a really well-treated cancer."


Sources:

  • Rivals unite to support Mountain Ridge basketball star battling cancer - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Batmobile stalls at auction by failing to meet the seller's minimum price
item.description:
A Batmobile built for Tim Burton's 1992 film Batman Returns went unsold at a Julien's auction Monday after bidding stalled at $3.25 million, below the seller's reserve. Julien's had estimated the car at $5 million to $7 million and hoped it would top the $4.6 million Batmobile record set in 2013.

A buyer would also have faced limits under an agreement with Warner Bros., such as keeping it "stationary when exhibited to the public" and getting approval for special events. Julien's called the car, one of three built for the film, "one of the most recognized and important cinematic vehicles in Hollywood history."


Sources:

  • Batmobile stalls at auction by failing to meet the seller's minimum price - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: R.J. Rico, Associated Press

item.title: Your flight was canceled. Who pays for dinner or the hotel?
item.description:
Under a federal Transportation Department rule, travelers whose flight is canceled, or whose domestic flight is expected to land three or more hours late, are owed an automatic refund if they decide not to fly. Help with meals and hotels is less certain and depends on each airline's own policies, and sometimes on the credit card used to buy the ticket.

Delta, which has a Salt Lake City hub, promises meals after three-hour delays within its control and hotel rooms for passengers stranded overnight. Katy Nastro of the Flighty app said the refund rule applies whether the cause is weather, an FAA ground stop or an airline's own decision.


Sources:

  • Your flight was canceled. Who pays for dinner or the hotel? - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt, KSL

item.title: Utah lawmakers eye another attempt to repeal law allowing developers to form cities
item.description:
A Utah legislative interim committee on Wednesday endorsed outgoing lawmaker Tiara Auxier's draft bill to fully repeal SB258, the 2024 pilot program letting private landowners in largely undeveloped areas petition to start new municipalities. Because Auxier lost her reelection bid, another legislator is likely to carry the bill when the general session opens in January.

As drafted, the repeal would also dissolve preliminary municipalities already approved, such as Echo Canyon in Grand County. Ivory Development president Chris Gamvroulas defended the law as an escape from "weaponized county government," while Sen. Calvin Musselman, who voted no, predicted, "A repeal is going to happen."


Sources:

  • Utah lawmakers eye another attempt to repeal law allowing developers to form cities - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Katie McKellar, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Utah man convicted of murder now accused of attacking officer at state prison
item.description:
Erik Orozco, 23, who pleaded guilty in 2022 to an Ogden murder and is already in prison, was charged Monday with aggravated assault targeting law enforcement and possessing a weapon as an inmate. Charging documents allege he came at a corrections officer from behind with a makeshift cutting weapon on July 26, leaving the officer with head lacerations; the officer was treated at a hospital.

The case is separate from a September attack on an officer at the Gunnison prison that led to a monthlong lockdown at two state facilities. According to the charges, Orozco told investigators he was "sick of how they were treating them and of the disrespect".


Sources:

  • Utah man convicted of murder now accused of attacking officer at state prison - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: New federal rule ends housing aid for some families
item.description:
A U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule finalized Nov. 10 will require every member of a household receiving federal housing aid to be verified as a citizen or eligible noncitizen starting Dec. 14. Mixed-status families that now pay higher rent to cover ineligible relatives will lose that option, and opponents estimate about 80,000 people could be displaced.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner said American taxpayers "will no longer foot the bill," but the department's own regulatory analysis projects no savings and up to $251 million in costs. Landlords get 90 days after the rule takes effect to comply.


Sources:

  • New federal rule ends housing aid for some families - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Cache County School District receives $990K grant to improve student literacy
item.description:
Intermountain Health has given the Cache County School District a three-year, $990,000 grant to strengthen reading and literacy programs across its schools. The district aims to have every third grader reading at benchmark by 2030, up from about 80% today.

Tabitha Bishop of Intermountain's Community Care Foundation said the plan stood out because it reached beyond students and educators to families and the wider community, calling it "really innovative and well thought out". District communications director Sheri Anderson said students who struggle to read find learning in subjects like health and science harder.


Sources:

  • Cache County School District receives $990K grant to improve student literacy - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Woman threatens to blow up trailer during standoff with police
item.description:
Beryl resident Brenda Tallerico, 58, was charged Monday with assaulting officers and other counts after allegedly threatening to blow up her trailer during a Sunday standoff with Iron County deputies. Deputies cut power and gas to the trailer, used chemical agents and finally breached the door to arrest her.

According to the affidavit, a relative told police she claimed to be filling the trailer with gas while waiting at the door with a torch. Her blood-alcohol level measured 0.34% at a hospital, and deputies reported finding "a large bundle of burnt matches" inside.


Sources:

  • Woman threatens to blow up trailer during standoff with police - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah board votes unanimously to certify the midterm election results
item.description:
Utah's State Board of Canvassers unanimously certified the general election results Monday, making official a vote that cost Republicans their supermajority in the Utah House. The GOP keeps control of both chambers, but after losing 16 House seats it will be without a veto-proof majority for the first time in close to three decades.

Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, whom several Republicans including Phil Lyman had asked to postpone certification, said the concerns they raised had "no merit". She said more than 90% of voters returned ballots by mail or drop box, adding that Utahns "prefer vote-by-mail".


Sources:

  • Utah board votes unanimously to certify the midterm election results - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: A stunning supermoon peaks this week. Here's what to know
item.description:
November's beaver moon, the first of three supermoons in a row, reaches peak fullness Tuesday morning, though NASA's Noah Petro says it will look full from Monday night through Wednesday evening. Petro says it should look roughly 17% bigger and 30% brighter than 2026's smallest full moon, enough that regular moon-watchers should notice.

Johns Hopkins professor Kevin Lewis suggests looking just after sunset, when the moon sits low and makes a striking sight. The Old Farmer's Almanac says December's cold moon on Dec. 23 will be the biggest and brightest supermoon of 2026.

  • A stunning supermoon peaks this week. Here's what to know - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Taylor Nicioli, CNN

item.title: Utah AG aims to jail Kalshi co-founders, arguing state will 'enforce its laws'
item.description:
Kalshi co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara have been summoned to appear for booking at the Salt Lake County Jail on Dec. 5 on 14 charges that include gambling promotion. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown says the prediction market app's founders will get no special treatment and had ample warning that their business is illegal in Utah.

"If anything, you can bet on Utah enforcing its laws," Brown said. Brown said Utah is uniquely positioned because only it and Hawaii outlaw all forms of gambling, and he noted the state constitution bars gambling "under any pretense".

  • Utah AG aims to jail Kalshi co-founders, arguing state will 'enforce its laws' - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Cameron Elliott, KSL

item.title: These Utah ski resorts open this week
item.description:
More Utah ski areas are set to open after last week's storms piled up to 3 feet of snow in the mountains, joining Brian Head and Solitude, which opened earlier. Brighton opens Tuesday, Nov. 24, for its 90th season, and Snowbird is opening two days ahead of its planned date.

Park City Mountain, which has picked up 38 inches of new snow, will run lifts out of both of its base areas. Snowbird general manager Dave Fields said the mountain "is in great shape for this time of year" and the resort wants to get people skiing when conditions allow.

  • These Utah ski resorts open this week - ksl.com
item.dc:creator: Dennis Romboy, Deseret News

item.title: Utah gas prices drop sharply over past month as economist predicts additional decline
item.description:
Utah's average price for regular gas fell to $3.83 a gallon Monday from $4.70 a month earlier, according to AAA, and Salt Lake County averaged $3.56. BYU economist Christian vom Lehn said prices could keep falling into January but likely won't return to the roughly $3 of a year ago.

Vom Lehn pointed to lower seasonal demand and more oil shipping out of the Middle East. Driver Missy Austin said prices are still too high: "I can't wait until they're so low that we can go on a vacation."


Sources:

  • Utah gas prices drop sharply over past month as economist predicts additional decline - ksl.com

item.title: Federal appeals court gives President Donald Trump a path to erasing hush money conviction
item.description:
A 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals panel on Monday revived President Donald Trump's bid to move his New York hush money case to federal court, reversing a lower-court ruling that kept it in state court. Should the case remain in federal court, Trump could argue that his 34-count conviction should be thrown out on presidential immunity grounds.

The panel told a federal judge to decide promptly whether the Manhattan federal court should keep the case, and the ruling begins a pause in Trump's parallel state court appeal. A Trump legal team spokesperson said the president "appreciates the 2nd Circuit's prompt and correct ruling," while the Manhattan District Attorney's Office declined to comment.

item.title: 'Don't borrow just to spend more': Utah financial expert warns about holiday financing offers
item.description:
Utah Valley University financial planning professor Shane Stewart is cautioning holiday shoppers against using zero-percent financing to spend more, saying such deals are better suited to restructuring or paying down debt. A 2026 WalletHub study found 78% of store cards with introductory zero-percent offers use deferred interest, which can charge interest back to the purchase date if any balance remains at the deadline.

WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo said store-card interest is reaching "record rates of up to 33%," and that shoppers focused on a deal may simply "sign on the dotted line" without carefully reviewing the terms.

item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera, KSL

item.title: Look inside the Utah prison plate plant — producing record license plate options
item.description:
Inmates at a plant inside the Utah State Correctional Facility make the license plates seen on Utah roads, averaging about 2,800 a day by production lead Jeffery Hernandez's count. Drivers now have 75 plate options to choose from, the most the state has ever offered, and the limited edition America 250 design is currently the top seller.

Only 20 inmates qualify for the jobs, which require a record free of violence and discipline problems and build skills for life after parole. Print tech Brian Urban said the work beats "staying back in the section" and lets workers "do something productive" there.

item.title: Trump orders the Army not to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa without court approval
item.description:
President Donald Trump on Monday ordered the military to hold off on detonating 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at an Iowa Army ammunition plant until a federal appeals court approves the plan. The Army, which had already moved the blast date three times amid health and environmental worries and was aiming for Wednesday, had no immediate comment.

Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand said Sunday that "No good options exist" because of earlier decisions, while Rodney Johnson, mayor of Middletown, where the plant sits, said it has to go forward "so we can move on with our lives."

item.title: Salt Lake Temple rededication date announced
item.description:
The First Presidency of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced Monday that the renovated Salt Lake Temple's rededication is set for Dec. 5, 2027. More tickets for the April-to-October 2027 open house will be released Tuesday through the Temple Square app and TempleSquare.org.

The first wave of open house reservations, 1 million in all, was claimed in under a day. The church leaders said the remodel and seismic retrofit are finished, and their letter said the temple will again let people take part in "sacred and eternal ordinances" for themselves and their ancestors.

item.title: Chinese neuroscientist at Princeton is held by ICE after detention at Washington airport
item.description:
ICE officers detained Eva Yi Xie, a Chinese doctoral student in neuroscience at Princeton, on Thursday at Reagan National Airport while she was heading back to New Jersey after a conference. The Department of Homeland Security says Xie overstayed a 2016 visa and will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

Her lawyer, Kerry Doyle, said Xie came to the U.S. with her family at 14 and has been waiting on an asylum application for years, but DHS says such an application "does not confer legal status." Graduate school dean Rodney Priestley called news of the detention "distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community" in a statement.

item.title: States sue Musk companies over flood of sexualized images made with AI chatbot Grok
item.description:
Democratic attorneys general in Virginia and Oregon sued several Elon Musk companies, including SpaceX and X, on Monday, alleging they launched the Grok chatbot without standard safeguards and fueled a flood of nonconsensual sexualized images. Virginia is seeking $2,500 for each willful violation of its consumer protection law plus a court order against further violations, and Oregon's separate suit makes a similar request.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in the suit that "weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature." SpaceX Super Intelligence, the SpaceX unit that developed Grok, called such content "abhorrent" and said it tightened protections once bad actors found ways to misuse the tool.

item.title: Utah Community Credit Union strike $7M partnership with Southern Utah University
item.description:
Southern Utah University and Utah Community Credit Union announced a multi-year, $7 million partnership on Thursday, one of the largest sponsorship deals in the university's history. The deal includes a UCCU branch with one-on-one financial coaching on campus, and the funding will also help pay for a football operations building and a digital billboard along I-15.

The partnership also aims to bring student jobs, and SUU President Mindy Benson said it reflects "a shared investment in our students' lives and long-term momentum" in a statement. The university said preparations for the branch and the new facilities will "begin soon."

item.title: Bill Clinton tells governors he hopes new political landscape can 'take some of the poison out'
item.description:
Former President Bill Clinton urged newly elected governors meeting in Park City to list concrete goals and work together on the country's biggest problems, including rebuilding trust. He spoke Thursday with Maryland Gov. Wes Moore at a National Governors Association forum attended by 33 new governors and 10 incumbents.

Clinton said he hoped the national mood could "take some of the poison out," while keeping healthy argument. He told them many won because voters thought they were "on the level" and in it for them.

item.title: Utah man wins 1st place for United States in The Great Wall of China Marathon
item.description:
Utah runner Michael Scott Peters placed fourth overall and first among Americans at The Great Wall of China Marathon, finishing in 4 hours and 50 minutes. He plans to run the Thanksgiving Point Half Marathon next and the Tokyo Marathon next year.

Peters, who signed up with only a month to prepare, described uneven, crumbling stairs made "extra slippery" by the race's first rain in 26 years. It was his 44th marathon and his first outside the country.

item.title: Anthropic's record IPO raises hopes for a charitable windfall that has nonprofits preparing to scale
item.description:
Anthropic's stock market debut at a record $1.5 trillion valuation has nonprofits preparing for a possible surge in donations from its founders and newly wealthy employees. The company plans to set aside 5% of its shares for a public benefit fund and its seven co-founders have pledged 80% of their equity, though many employees cannot sell or give away most of their stock before next spring.

GiveDirectly CEO Nick Allardice described "cautious optimism" about the preparations. Renaissance Philanthropy president Kumar Garg warned that putting philanthropic money to work is not automatic.
