item.title: New 'Toxic Hall of Shame' includes Publix, Trader Joe's and McDonald's
item.description:
Toxic-Free Future's latest retailer report card, shared first with CNN, put 16 major retailers including Trader Joe's, Publix, McDonald's, Wayfair and Williams-Sonoma in its Toxic Hall of Shame with F grades for failing to cut hazardous chemicals and plastics, while Apple got an A, with A- grades for Ikea, Target and Sephora. The average grade was a D+, only 10% of retailers reported measurable reduction goals compared with 44% in 2024, and Walmart and Whole Foods posted the steepest declines to land at C, though Whole Foods said an internal error kept some of its information from reaching the group by the deadline. McDonald's sent CNN a report showing it had reached over 99% of its 2025 target for cutting added fluorinated compounds, but Toxic-Free Future's Mike Schade noted it set no new goals for other problem chemicals and called PFAS "just the tip of the toxic iceberg".

item.title: Vincent van Gogh painting sells for $190 million, smashing auction record
item.description:
Van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs, which shows a burst of chestnut trees at Auvers-sur-Oise from his final months, sold for more than $190 million at Sotheby's in New York on Wednesday after a three-minute bidding contest, far above his previous auction record of $117.2 million. The sale came days after heirs of Samuel Fischer, a Jewish publisher in 1930s Berlin, said the work had been sold under Nazi-era financial pressure; Sotheby's said its provenance research did not support that but announced Tuesday it had reached an agreement with them on undisclosed terms. The 12 works from the Blaquier-Arrieta family's rarely seen collection, which Sotheby's Helena Newman called "a mini Musée d'Orsay" and which the family never lent to museums, brought in almost $412 million, including over $111 million for Cézanne's Arlequin.

item.title: Park City Council votes to table long-discussed housing project
item.description:
After roughly a decade of discussion, the Park City Council voted 3-2 against a Brinshore Development mixed-use project for the Bonanza Park area that would have brought around 90 affordable housing units along with a cafe, retail and outdoor space, and a parking structure. Residents had objected to added traffic and the building's proposed height, and were also upset that the Kimball Arts Center decided in 2025 not to move near the site. Councilwoman Molly Miller lamented the lack of support for affordable housing, warning that service workers will suffer if it keeps disappearing, while Councilman Ed Parigian, objecting that people can sign a piece of paper and think they're on the council, called it "a crazy way to run a town".

item.title: Expert: FBI FLASH advisory highlights AI developments in cyber threats
item.description:
An FBI FLASH advisory posted by the agency's Dallas office warns that state actors and cybercriminals have used ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, to automate attacks, saying it can get from initial targeting to privileged access "in under three hours". Adam Marre, chief information security officer at Arctic Wolf, said the tool was built for defenders who probe organizations for weaknesses, and that while its developer has pulled it, copies of the open-source software remain in circulation. Marre said attackers are finding vulnerabilities at a scale far beyond prior years and urged companies to pair basics like password managers and phishing awareness with stronger defenses, possibly AI-based ones, adding, "Now everybody has to take cybersecurity seriously."

item.title: Utah lawmakers unveil draft legislation aimed at regulating police use of surveillance technology
item.description:
A draft bill presented Wednesday to the Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice Interim Committee would require police agencies to publicly post policies for technology such as automatic license plate readers, run quarterly internal audits and discipline employees who misuse the systems. It leaves out the two safeguards privacy advocates have pressed hardest for, independent audits and a warrant requirement for non-emergency searches; Sen. Calvin Musselman said separate bills would handle specific policies, and Libertas Institute privacy analyst Emily Grimmius said "external audits are much needed for public trust". The proposal comes a week after a KSL Investigation found a former Tooele County detective had used the department's plate-reader system to look up the vehicle of the estranged husband of a woman the detective was seeing, misconduct that a routine audit did not uncover.

item.title: Promise that started at age 11 grows into Thanksgiving meals for 3,600 Utah families
item.description:
Thanksgiving Heroes, which grew out of a promise founder Rob Adams made to his mother at age 11 after others helped his struggling family, is expected to provide Thanksgiving meals to 3,600 Utah families through a Saturday distribution at a Draper warehouse. Golf tournaments, concerts and other events pay for the groceries, and Adams said planning that once began around Halloween now starts at the beginning of the year. Donations are behind this year as food prices climb and the need grows, Adams said, though "every year the miracle shows up."

item.description:
Ahead of the Salt Lake Temple's six-month open house starting next April, the Church History Museum on Temple Square has opened three exhibits, including artifacts from the temple's April 1893 dedication such as the original Tabernacle Choir music stand, dedication tickets and attendees' journal entries. One by One gathers 55 personal faith stories from 40 countries, Fitly Framed Together traces the craftsmen and members who built the temple, and All Nations Shall Flow Into It displays art from around the world. Curator Emily Utt said the public got about two hours inside before the 1893 dedication, with a couple hundred people admitted, and added, "We want the world to come and be with us."

item.title: The etiquette you're not thinking about: Healthy ways to talk about food this holiday season
item.description:
KSL health contributor Miki Eberhardt says holiday etiquette should extend beyond table manners to how families talk about food and bodies. Weight changes can stem from grief, anxiety, illness or disordered eating, so a weight-loss compliment can land badly; "You could be praising someone's really hard thing," Eberhardt said, recommending a hug and a warm greeting instead. Eberhardt also said other people's food choices shouldn't become a group topic and urged letting each guest decide what and how much goes on the plate, adding, "We don't wanna be micromanagers."

item.title: Advisory issued for Utah's mountains after Wasatch Front receives first snow of season
item.description:
Utah's latest storm brought the Wasatch Front its first valley snow of the season and piled 19 inches on Alta and 18 on Snowbird, keeping both on track to open next week. Salt Lake City officially recorded 0.7 inches Tuesday, 40 days earlier in the calendar than its first measurable snow last year, when the capital collected just 3.7 inches all season, its lowest total since record-keeping began in 1874; KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson said "considering last year, we're happy to see this". The National Weather Service has posted winter weather advisories for northern and southern mountain ranges and Wasatch Back towns ahead of a second system expected Thursday into Saturday, with valley rain possibly turning to snow along the Wasatch Front by Friday afternoon.

item.title: Dash camera footage shows Summit County deputies using PIT maneuver in chase
item.description:
A court ordered an arrest warrant Monday for Derek Trevor Holland, 33, after Adult Probation and Parole determined he had broken his probation terms; newly obtained dash camera footage shows a Summit County deputy using a PIT maneuver to end his flight in a stolen car. According to a police affidavit, the Dec. 9, 2025, pursuit on state Route 224 started with a stop over an unlit license plate and topped 100 mph, and the car turned out to have been stolen from Salt Lake City. Holland pleaded guilty to a reduced attempted theft/receiving charge and got a suspended prison term with three years' probation, but has since contested part of the restitution, arguing he admitted only to possessing the car.

item.title: Takeaways from Mullin's testimony on cyber outages, the Texas-LSU flight and immigration
item.description:
Testifying Wednesday before the House Homeland Security Committee, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and intelligence director Jay Clayton insisted that the past week's outages at Microsoft, the FAA, banks and an NSA network were unrelated and not a cyberattack, with Mullin saying he was "98% confident" adversaries weren't involved. Mullin also defended flying to the LSU-Texas game on Saturday while travelers were still stranded by the ground stop, saying the trip had been planned for weeks, that he paid for it, and that canceling with the airspace open might have signaled distrust. On immigration, he said every ICE officer now serving has passed a full background check and anyone lacking one or the full 13 weeks of training is on leave, and when Rep. LaMonica McIver accused him of killing people, he dismissed it as "your opinion".

item.title: University of Utah bringing continuing education program to Asia campus
item.description:
The University of Utah's continuing education program, which dates to 1906 and serves more than 30,000 learners a year, launched Nov. 5 at the U.'s Asia Campus in Incheon, South Korea, the university's first overseas campus, opened in 2013. Ava Choi, who directs continuing education at the Asia Campus, said the courses won't simply be imported from Utah but were designed jointly around South Korean workforce needs, local interests and growing industries, and a university release said the offerings are meant for learners whether or not they are seeking a degree. Randy McCrillis, the U.'s vice provost for continuing education, said the expansion advances the U.'s international mission of "making the university's expertise available to people wherever they are."

item.title: Deportations are up and arrests of Utah immigrants are also on the rise, data shows
item.description:
ICE arrests ending in detention in Utah totaled 7,545 from January 2025 through early August, according to Deportation Data Project figures, with the monthly average climbing from around 285 in the first half of 2025 to 480 from January through July 2026, compared with about 118 a month in 2024. Detainees without criminal convictions grew from 29.2% of Utah detentions in March 2025 to 54.9% last July, while arrests through 287(g) agreements with local law enforcement stayed a small, relatively steady slice after early jumps: 294 since July 2025, most of them in Weber and Washington counties. The data arrives as DHS reports a record 483,200 removals nationwide in fiscal 2026; within Utah, West Valley City led with 1,094 arrests, just ahead of Salt Lake City's 1,025.

item.title: Trump plans separate talks with Putin alongside their 3-way meeting with Xi in China
item.description:
President Donald Trump plans a one-on-one meeting with Vladimir Putin in China on Thursday, on top of a scheduled three-way session with Xi Jinping, a U.S. official told the AP, in what would be their first talks since last year's Alaska meeting failed to yield a Ukraine deal. Trump said he wants to discuss nuclear arms limits and ending the war, saying that "it's very close to getting it done," although his aides had said beforehand that Ukraine was off the agenda and analysts expect no major breakthroughs. The trip to the APEC summit in Shenzhen, where Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac, has been shadowed by outages at Microsoft, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase and an NSA network, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero" evidence they were linked to one another or to rival nations or hackers.

item.title: How Iran is using social media to exploit US vulnerabilities
item.description:
Alongside Iran's low-cost drones, social media has become a growing asymmetrical threat in the U.S. conflict with Iran: this month the Iranian Embassy in South Africa used X to tell two U.S. Navy officers "We will find you," and another post last weekend mocked Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent and Pete Hegseth over their relocation to military installations following reported threats. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has directed Navy and Marine Corps members to make their accounts private and delete posts that reveal military ties or family routines, writing that "Force protection" is everyone's responsibility. Separately, Senators John Curtis and Mark Kelly said the Army reversed a policy, in place since last June, that barred Dugway and Yuma proving grounds from running their own social media accounts, which the senators had warned would undermine public safety communications.

item.title: 312 pounds of meth seized in UHP drug bust
item.description:
Charles Terry, 63, of Chicago, faces drug distribution charges in 4th District Court after a Utah Highway Patrol stop in Millard County that is believed to rank among the largest drug busts in recent state history. According to a booking affidavit, a trooper pulled over Terry's Jeep Cherokee on I-15 on Oct. 28 over window tint, grew suspicious of three large suitcases for what the driver described as a few days of gambling and shopping in Las Vegas, and after a K-9 alerted found 312 pounds of meth plus two kilos of cocaine/fentanyl in vacuum-sealed packaging. The affidavit also cites "an extensive criminal history" going back to 1983, with past charges that include murder and a prior federal drug case, though details on the murder case weren't immediately available.

item.title: Utah receives $11M from Department of Energy for grid infrastructure projects
item.description:
The U.S. Department of Energy awarded Utah $11 million for its Grid Resilience grant program, part of $967 million handed out nationwide and a follow-up to an $18 million award in 2024 that paid for 11 projects stretching from Box Elder to Washington counties. Utilities, including municipalities and co-ops, can apply starting in 2027, with the required match tied to each utility's annual electricity sales. Emy Lesofski, director of the Utah Office of Energy Development, said producing affordable power is "only half the equation" because the state must also deliver it, while Senate President J. item.title: Kilby Block Party completes its 2027 lineup with a pair of Best New Artist nominees
item.description:

State, which will replace the Avenues hospital, but the project still awaits a design review by the city's planning commission, which has yet to schedule a vote. After commissioners raised concerns at a rocky meeting last month, architects made the outpatient pharmacy more accessible, let the public reach a coffee shop and bistro from the street without passing hospital security, and added a "functional greenhouse"; Intermountain is also reviewing exterior materials. A family that moved to Utah from South Africa went sledding in the mountains to see snow for the first time, as the season's first major storm turned the Wasatch high country white and sent skiers hiking uphill for early runs before resorts are fully open. One skier called the early snow great compared with last year, and Reef Heikkila predicted "it will be a good season" if it keeps up. item.title: Paramedic mother responds to accident that claimed her son's life in central Utah
item.description:
Sevier County paramedic Tricia Mumford was among the crews answering a Monday evening call in Sigurd and, according to Sheriff Nathan Curtis, realized only after the patient was freed that it was her 28-year-old son, Logan Mumford, pinned when a car slipped off a scissor jack as he helped a woman from his ward replace an alternator. A neighbor who had gone across the street for a floor jack and better lighting could not pull him out, and deputies used that jack to free him before he was flown with severe head injuries to Utah Valley Medical Center; he later died. Fellow paramedic Tyla Northrup, a friend of Tricia Mumford's, said "Nobody can fathom working on their own son," and called Logan Mumford a person who was always ready to help anyone.

item.title: Salt Lake City passes 6-month pause on data centers, seeks future adjustments
item.description:
The Salt Lake City Council unanimously approved a pause of up to six months on new data centers Tuesday, giving the city, and possibly the state, time to write rules before it expires in mid-May. The measure appears to respond to a little-detailed data center proposed in the Northpoint neighborhood, where Florida-based Qlevr LLC sought an air quality permit listing diesel-fired emergency generators, and Councilwoman Victoria Petro, who represents the area, called the project "a thorn in my side". Mayor Erin Mendenhall called it a "healthy pause", saying the city's zoning never contemplated data centers at the scale now being proposed, and the vote follows a Salt Lake County moratorium that covered only unincorporated land.

item.title: Ohio man who sexually abused Utah minor given 45 years in prison
item.description:
A federal judge on Tuesday gave an Ohio man 45 years in prison, followed by probation for life, in a case involving a young Utah girl. Wade S. Christofferson, 73, pleaded guilty in July to a coercion and enticement count; prosecutors say he spent about six months mailing the child sexually coded letters, and that he admitted abusing her during past Utah visits after her father confronted him over inappropriate behavior seen on a FaceTime call. Dominick S. Gerace II, the top federal prosecutor for Ohio's southern district, said the evidence showed "a longstanding sexual interest in children that spanned decades".

item.title: Democrats flipped 9 US Senate seats — the most in almost 70 years
item.description:
Democrats will hold 56 of 100 Senate seats when the new Congress starts in January after Mary Peltola unseated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, the party's ninth pickup and its best midterm showing in the chamber since 1958. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," and the party also retook the House, gaining 42 seats as of Tuesday. The Senate has usually been more insulated than the House from midterm swings against the party in power, though second-term midterms are typically rougher.

item.title: Apple joins a parade of technology hiccups in recent days
item.description:
Apple said an internal update caused outages Tuesday that fully knocked out Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare and disrupted iCloud sign-ins, though many systems were back up by the time it issued a statement. The trouble capped a run of breakdowns that included a United Airlines system outage of more than 90 minutes that delayed departures Monday, a JPMorgan Chase technical issue the same day that rippled into other major banks and Zelle, last week's global Microsoft outage hitting Outlook, Teams and Copilot, and the FAA network malfunction behind a nationwide ground stop. Marriott also appeared to have reservation and check-in problems, according to Reddit users, and Downdetector showed an outage there, while United said it saw no sign of a cybersecurity link and Chase and Microsoft both said a cyberattack was not behind their problems.

item.title: Intermountain Health breaks ground on new LDS Hospital in downtown Salt Lake City
item.description:
On Tuesday, Intermountain Health held a groundbreaking for a new LDS Hospital on the roughly eight-acre former Sears site at 745 S. State Street, planning a 10-story hospital of more than 521,000 square feet plus a seven-story medical office building; the downtown campus will eventually replace the hospital's longtime home in the Avenues. The downtown campus is to offer emergency, trauma and intensive care, cancer, heart, surgical, and women's and newborn services, a Level II NICU and a public plaza, and Intermountain estimates it will support about 2,000 jobs and more than $1.1 billion a year in local economic impact. The Avenues hospital, open since 1905, will keep running in the meantime with its future still undecided, while LDS Hospital President Heather Wall described the move as "bringing that excellence forward".

item.title: Millburn defeats Lee in Davis County Commission race; Lee backer calls for probe
item.description:
Unaffiliated former commissioner Brett Millburn beat Republican Susan Lee for a Davis County Commission seat by 55,200 votes to 54,788 in results certified Tuesday, but Lee's campaign manager, Jason Sanders, has asked state and county officials to investigate whether Millburn broke Utah's electioneering law. Sanders points to Millburn's Oct. 20 remarks about his candidacy during public comment at Fruit Heights and Woods Cross council meetings, held in buildings with ballot drop boxes during the mail-in voting period, and said the effort isn't aimed at reversing the result. Millburn's attorney, David Irvine, said election law attorneys read the statute as covering campaigning near polling places or drop boxes on Election Day and called the complaint "the last stand of a desperate and disappointed candidate."

item.title: Utah's crackdown on online betting expands with lawsuit against casino site
item.description:
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Division of Consumer Protection have sued the companies behind Stake, the world's biggest online casino, alleging that its sweepstakes-style model, in which users buy a virtual currency that converts back to cash one-to-one, is illegal gambling under Utah law. The 3rd District Court complaint, the state's third against a betting platform in the past month, says Stake blocks residents of 25 states but not Utah and courts young audiences with influencers and cartoon-themed slots, and it seeks restitution and penalties "well in excess" of $300,000 each. "You don't get to legalize gambling in Utah simply by using clever marketing tricks," Brown said.

item.title: Unsheltered Utah expands winter shelter program to serve more neighbors in need
item.description:
Rather than opening only on Code Blue nights, when overnight lows are expected to hit 18 degrees or colder, Unsheltered Utah will run overnight shelter on a regular schedule this winter, Mondays and Thursdays, in partnership with First United Methodist Church and St. Mark's Cathedral. Executive director Merinda Cutler said last year's mild winter meant the group opened just 14 of the 30 nights it was prepared for, and that the church's fellowship hall takes in 73 adults, pets included, with cots, a hot meal and survival supplies. The nonprofit is looking for overnight volunteers and donations, including for a hotel program that, Cutler said, gives families a few nights' stay because the shelter isn't safe for them.

  • Unsheltered Utah expands winter shelter program to serve more neighbors in need - ksl.com

item.title: Board of Peace warning of Gaza ceasefire collapse without immediate action
item.description:
In its first annual assessment to the U.N. Security Council, the Board of Peace overseeing the U.S.-brokered Gaza ceasefire warned the deal could collapse, citing continued Israeli strikes, Hamas military activity and Israel's failure so far to let the board's interim technocratic administration start work in the territory. Rebuilding, Hamas' disarmament and an Israeli pullout all hinge on an international stabilization force whose deployment has been held up as a result, the report says, and it urges the Security Council to lean on both sides to end the delays. "A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely," the report said.

item.title: 'Keep Utah Monumental' campaign launches after cuts to Bears Ears, Grand Staircase-Escalante
item.description:
The Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance on Tuesday launched a Keep Utah Monumental campaign of billboards, digital ads and community organizing aimed at holding Gov. Spencer Cox and Utah's congressional delegation accountable for President Donald Trump's July order cutting Bears Ears to about 121,000 acres and Grand Staircase-Escalante to about 182,000. Cox has said the cuts leave other protections in place while making the monuments "more manageable," but a Deseret News-Hinckley Institute of Politics poll found 56% of Utahns oppose the reductions and 29% support them. Executive director Scott Braden said the midterms show Utah is "changing and changing fast" and that, come January, the delegation will include a member committed to restoring the monuments; that member is Ben McAdams, winner of the race for the 1st Congressional District.

  • 'Keep Utah Monumental' campaign launches after cuts to Bears Ears, Grand Staircase-Escalante - ksl.com

item.title: State senator given corrective actions following workplace discrimination investigation
item.description:
Utah Senate leadership will deny Sen. Kathleen Riebe, D-Cottonwood Heights, any Senate staff or legislative intern, move her office away from Senate staff and require more harassment-prevention training, among four corrective actions imposed after a Parsons Behle & Latimer investigation found she "more likely than not" violated policies on workplace harassment and discrimination. The legislative staffer involved said Riebe made racially charged comments and remarks about the staffer's clothing, body and pregnancy, and the Senate Minority Caucus voted Nov. 3 to remove Riebe and called for a resignation. Riebe's attorney, Ryan McConnell, dismissed the claims as hearsay, called the investigation retaliatory and said the law firm had donated to Sen. Luz Escamilla, whom Riebe had intended to challenge for Senate minority leader.

  • State senator given corrective actions following workplace discrimination investigation - ksl.com

item.title: Nvidia chairman says board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
item.description:
Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said Tuesday the board does not intend to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO, hours after Huang, who left last week following revelations of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, posted that he would be "honored to answer these calls" if the board decided his return was in the company's best interest. Huang's comeback bid has drawn support from Elon Musk, President Donald Trump and a petition signed by current and former employees and investors, and key House lawmakers said Huang has voluntarily agreed to transcribed interviews; he is set to appear before the committees on Dec. 1 as Nvidia's chip sales draw growing national scrutiny. Nvidia's third-quarter results, which made no mention of the ouster, beat expectations with more than $116 billion in revenue, double a year earlier, and the company said it is forming a board committee to oversee national security and trade compliance.

item.title: How 'Grand Theft Auto VI' is hijacking fans' lives
item.description:
With Grand Theft Auto VI arriving at midnight Thursday after more than a decade in development and two delays, fans are clearing their calendars: Oregon software engineer Malcolm Bixby is taking two weeks off with a spreadsheet that schedules play, sleep, meals and showers, and one Army battalion in Georgia is giving soldiers who reenlist four days off around the release. The Washington Post reported the game had already passed $1 billion in sales a week before launch, and RIT's José P. Zagal credits part of its worldwide pull to its "funhouse mirror" vision of America. Ciara Singleton, who dressed as the new female protagonist Lucia over Halloween weekend, rejected the idea that gamers are loners, saying "It's a community."

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ celebrates 10 years of Light the World Giving Machines with new locations
item.description:
At a Temple Square event Tuesday marking 10 years of the Church of Jesus Christ's Giving Machines, the vending-style kiosks where people buy meals, school supplies or livestock for those in need, Sister Tamara W. Runia said the program has grown from one Salt Lake City location in November 2017 to 145 machines in 28 countries this year, "the most ever." The event also celebrated $70 million raised so far, and this year's 25 new locations include a truck-mounted mobile machine in Lima, Peru, while Elder Jeremiah J. Morgan said more than 500 nonprofits have partnered with the church to supply the machines. Miriam Murdoch of Lifting Hands International described a woman in a Ugandan refugee camp for whom two donated goats meant both food and income, calling such gifts tools that help people climb out of poverty and displacement.

item.title: 'Broken Cowboy': New documentary highlights paralyzed artist who turns scrap metal into art
item.description:
Washington County artist Matt Clark, left paralyzed at 17 in 1979 when the pickup he was working under rolled down a driveway and broke his neck, defied doctors' prediction that he would probably be lucky to live three years, taught himself to weld again and has since made thousands of sculptures from discarded scrap metal. Clark, who had competed in calf roping at the high school national finals, sees the work as a metaphor for his own recovery, saying broken pieces have the potential "to become a new entity", and he gives each of his horse sculptures a heart as a final touch. A documentary about him by Emmy-winning filmmaker and former football player Phil Tuckett, Broken Cowboy: The Matt Clark Story, will be screened by DOCUTAH at Utah Tech University on Nov. 21.

item.title: Glasses, shirt buttons will be examined to stop cheating in South Korea's college entrance exams
item.description:
With more than 550,000 people sitting the Suneung on Thursday, South Korea is answering a wave of AI-assisted cheating with 8,400 extra supervisors, inspections of test-takers' glasses, stickers over shirt buttons and a nationwide phone alert designed to expose hidden devices. Prime Minister Han Seongsook said the exam ban for cheaters will grow from one year to 10 and that companies running AI chatbots have agreed to help with post-exam investigations. The crackdown followed a confession from the tax accountant exam's top scorer that he got answers from AI through a hidden microcamera and smartphone, and Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said "we are in a situation where excessive measures are necessary".

item.title: FAA temporarily stops router installations connected to air travel stoppage
item.description:
The FAA has paused new Juniper router installations and disabled the ones already in service after technicians tied last week's nationwide ground stop to a newly installed router in El Dorado, Arkansas, leaving older Cisco routers, in service for 25 years, to carry the network while the cause is investigated. Senate Commerce Democrats told Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that pinpointing the device doesn't explain why it failed, while Juniper owner Hewlett Packard Enterprise says that, as far as it knows, the device worked as the installer configured it and "did not fail or act improperly". The scrutiny comes as the Trump administration asks lawmakers for $50.1 billion to modernize air travel, and Bernstein analysts estimated the outage and recovery cost the four largest U.S. carriers a combined $345 million.

item.title: Do school phone bans help students learn? So far, gains are 'modest'
item.description:
A Harvard-led analysis of test scores from 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools found that locking phones in pouches for the whole school day produced "modest" academic gains, worth about one to two extra weeks of learning a year, which the researchers say could build up over time. Stanford economist Thomas Dee, an author of a May National Bureau of Economic Research study that found close to zero effect on test scores, called the early results "largely disappointing" and said he isn't comfortable projecting long-term gains from such small estimates. San Diego State psychologist Jean Twenge said bans often aren't enforced in practice and students can still turn to laptops, while Harvard's Thomas Kane said the impact of phone use outside school can't be answered until social media companies share their data.

item.title: He plans to run 11,350 miles around the country. He's taking his family and God with him
item.description:
Orem's Chris Avery, whose daily running streak dates to Jan. 9, 2022, plans to run a 50K every day of 2027 on an 11,350-mile loop around the perimeter of the United States, starting and ending in Tempe, Arizona, while his wife, Melanie, and their two young children follow in an RV. The couple, members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, are paying for the trip themselves, selling their possessions and raising money for three charities, including the Gary Sinise Foundation, though they worry about running out of money. Avery, who says he hates running, describes the effort as a shared family adventure grounded in faith: "it's me, my wife and God" and now the kids, he said.

item.title: Salt Lake County Council to consider resolution to protect Dimple Dell Regional Park
item.description:
Salt Lake County Council members are expected to vote Tuesday on a resolution backing protection of the 643-acre Dimple Dell Regional Park in Sandy, a week after the city dropped a proposed environmental impact study of a Highland Drive extension that drew concerns from hundreds of residents. Joyce Walker, president of the nonprofit Dimple Dell Preservation Community, wants a land trust or stronger preservation measures and argues a wide road and bridge through the park would not ease traffic on 1300 East and 700 East and could instead draw Utah County commuters through the community. Sandy resident Bryan Chamberlain countered that the study would have weighed several corridors, not only a bridge, and said, "I don't understand why we're not doing it."

item.title: Tech company says it can mine lithium from Great Salt Lake without consuming any water
item.description:
Lilac Solutions, which ran a portable pilot plant on Great Salt Lake's northeastern shore for seven months and recently won a $100 million Department of Energy grant, says its fifth-generation system uses ceramic-type beads to pull lithium from brine and then returns the brine to the lake instead of relying on evaporation ponds. Engineering vice president Mark Mulligan said a full-scale plant of about 20 acres would produce 5,000 tons a year of lithium carbonate equivalent, matching current U.S. output, and would operate for 20 years before its equipment must be removed. Grow the Flow's Ben Abbott called the approach "a real proven technology" that has yet to be scaled up anywhere in the U.S., and said moving some of the lake's existing evaporative extraction to it could save anywhere from tens of thousands to a couple hundred thousand acre-feet of water.

item.title: Utah House Democrats elect new leader after big election gains
item.description:
Utah House Democrats have picked Rep. Jen Dailey-Provost, D-Salt Lake City, a public health professional who has served in the Legislature since 2019, as minority leader, replacing Angela Romero, who had sought another term, as the caucus prepares to double in size after flipping Republican seats and ending the GOP's House supermajority for the first time in decades. The choice, announced late Monday, came 10 days after Republicans kept Mike Schultz as House speaker, and Senate Democrats also kept Luz Escamilla as their minority leader. In a statement, the new House leaders listed the cost of living, the shrinking Great Salt Lake, education and government accountability as priorities, adding "These are not partisan issues".

item.title: 'This is only a test': Tuesday's emergency alert test comes at anxious moment in the US
item.description:
FEMA will run a legally mandated nationwide Emergency Alert System test around 2:20 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday, a roughly one-minute message on radio and broadcast, cable and satellite TV that, unlike the 2023 test, will not reach cell phones. Stelter writes that the long-scheduled drill arrives as a string of glitches has left Americans uneasy about fragile tech systems and is already being worked into some social media conspiracy theories, prompting FEMA to post on X: "No blackouts, no secret emergencies." A 2015 law requires a nationwide test no less often than every three years, and FEMA says it could be pushed to Dec. 3 if a real emergency or major weather event happens that day.

item.title: Idaho voters enshrined English in its Constitution. Now come the questions
item.description:
More than 63% of Idaho voters on Nov. 3 approved House Joint Resolution 6, a 50-word constitutional amendment naming English the state language that constitutional law professor McKay Cunningham says will supersede the 538-word official-language statute while appearing to cut its "really big exceptions". The attorney general's office hasn't analyzed the measure and the state Education Department hasn't issued school guidance, leaving advocates such as Idaho Hispanic Foundation director Mari Ramos seeking answers on whether families will keep access to translated information and services. Sen. Brian Lenney, who carried the bill, has argued the old exemptions were far too broad and that learning English is a ticket to full membership, while Jerome's Benjamin Reed called the measure "a dog whistle" to Idaho's most virulent racists.

item.title: Trump appeals to state and federal courts to erase hush money conviction
item.description:
A three-judge 2nd U.S. Circuit panel questioned Trump's lawyer and a Manhattan prosecutor for over an hour Monday about moving the president's 34-count hush money conviction out of New York state court and into federal court, where he could seek dismissal on presidential immunity grounds, and did not rule immediately. Attorney Robert Giuffra Jr. asked the judges to act quickly and halt the state Appellate Division, which heard Trump's parallel appeal Nov. 5 and has yet to decide, but Chief Judge Raymond J. Lohier Jr. said Giuffra's proposed route through a federal district judge amounted to "an entire procedural mechanism that I don't see anywhere authorized by Congress". Steven Wu of the Manhattan District Attorney's Office urged the panel to uphold Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein's August ruling against Trump and keep the case in state court.

item.title: Utah search and rescue teams preparing for winter storm, urging backcountry travelers to do the same
item.description:
With a major storm expected to start piling snow on Utah's mountains this week, firefighter Josh Hicken spent Monday swapping summer rescue gear for winter equipment, saying search and rescue teams think about missions differently once the cold sets in. Hicken, who has trained search and rescue crews for 15 years, said a common mistake is packing only for the outing people plan rather than what could go wrong, and he urged backcountry visitors to carry an emergency shelter, extra layers and food in case conditions rapidly deteriorate. "I think we've been spoiled and we've forgotten that it's Utah," Hicken said.

item.title: Watchdog group seeks halt in use of license plate readers, accuses UDOT of overreach
item.description:
The Utah Civic Compact on Monday asked Gov. Spencer Cox to have UDOT pause vendor-owned license plate readers along state highways until the Legislature regulates them, saying the agency exceeded its authority with a rule that effectively licensed Flock Safety statewide. The group estimates at least 1,000 readers operate in Utah, perhaps half covered by the UDOT rule, though it says solid data has been hard to get. UDOT spokesman John Gleason said the agency's role is limited to permitting law enforcement equipment and ensuring safe installation, that privacy concerns "are not UDOT questions" and that UDOT is still identifying how many cameras sit in its right-of-way, while Cox's office deferred to UDOT.

item.title: British women receive pardons for past abortion convictions
item.description:
Women in Britain convicted under an 1861 law for ending their own pregnancies were automatically pardoned Monday, some posthumously, following Parliament's vote last year to decriminalize abortion, and women who had received police cautions were also pardoned, while arrests and investigations were removed from records. The government gave no count, but Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, sponsor of the decriminalization amendment, said more than 100 women had been investigated by police in the five years before the vote, including some who had miscarriages or stillbirths, and described suspects being "dragged from hospital beds to police cells". Anti-abortion groups opposed the change, which followed high-profile cases such as the 2023 jailing of Carla Foster, who was freed a month later by an appeals court that called for "compassion, not punishment."

item.title: The companies Utah consumers complain about the most
item.description:
Of 307 Utah consumer complaints obtained by The Utah Investigative Journalism Project under a 2024 law that makes some complaints public, Action Heating, Cooling and Plumbing drew the largest share at 45%, followed by Meta and Private Label Accelerator, while Emerald Pools & Spas topped disputed funds at more than $1.6 million of over $5 million total. Complaints described a bedridden woman billed thousands for unclogging, solar panels that were never switched on and a residential cruise that appeared unlikely ever to sail; separately, Action's lawyers dispute the state's allegations and say complaint counts aren't a "reliable or fair measure" of a company's record. Blake Young, the consumer protection division's former deputy commissioner, said the law has had little public effect so far and warned that "AI is making it very, very easy for scammers to operate".

item.title: Pope Leo's return to Latin America reveals the missionary message of his papacy
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV's 12-day South American tour, coming weeks after lung cancer surgery, drew an estimated 12 million-plus people to events in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, and his relentless schedule eased doubts about his health for now. In Peru, where Leo spent about two decades as a missionary and bishop and still holds citizenship, crowds in his former diocese of Chiclayo hailed him as one of their own, and he told a Lima Mass that "The Peruvian people are my people too" before flying home Monday. CNN's Lamb writes that the trip, along with Leo's public U.S. midterm vote and his urging of Argentina's president to safeguard democracy, casts the first American pope as a prominent defender of democracy and a pastor still most at ease on the church's margins.

item.title: Jury finds 2 men guilty of murder in death of 18-year-old at Mount Olympus trailhead
item.description:
Jurors on Friday convicted Mateo Heriberto Martinez, 23, and Alex Ruiz-Martinez, 21, of murder, aggravated kidnapping and other felonies with gang enhancements in the August 2024 death of 18-year-old Naod Welday, who was found dead in a car at the Mount Olympus trailhead after, according to the district attorney's statement, six to eight men forced their way into the locked vehicle where Welday and a friend had sheltered. District Attorney Sim Gill said the three young men who were attacked had come to the U.S. as refugees and that Welday was "simply trying to enjoy the view of Salt Lake Valley with some friends" when he was killed. Sentencing is set for Jan. 14; a 17-year-old was already convicted in juvenile court, two others still face the same charges, and three people are accused of helping hide a vehicle.

item.title: Utah women business leaders honored for building companies and opening doors
item.description:
Minky Couture founder and CEO Sandi Sumner Hendry, a longtime elementary teacher who began selling blankets from her car trunk after a hospitalized daughter asked for a soft one, received the Salt Lake Chamber's 2026 ATHENA Leadership Award at its 50th annual Women & Business Conference. Hendry, whose company now has six Utah stores and donates blankets to premature babies in hospitals and to veterans, said in her speech, "I feel a responsibility and desire to give back." Six others received Pathfinder Awards, including Sally Steed of the Deseret News, Abby Osborne of the Utah 2034 Winter Games organizing committee and Victoria Petro of the Utah Hispanic Chamber of Commerce.

item.title: Lindon teen battling cancer for second time hopes to make Christmas special for others
item.description:
Lindon 13-year-old Jake Braithwaite, declared cancer-free in March after chemotherapy for the rare gray zone lymphoma, learned six months later that the cancer was back and is scheduled to enter the hospital Nov. 24 to begin a stem cell transplant, a stay that could last through Christmas. Inspired by the support neighbors and friends have shown his family, Jake is gathering holiday gifts and donations for a pair of refugee families, one with a boy close to his age, and said "shopping for someone else your age, it's been even better for me". The family plans to brighten his hospital room with lights, a small tree and Snoopy decorations, and his mother, Hillary Braithwaite, said the project has helped take his mind off treatment.

item.title: SUU adjunct professor breaks world record, brings attention to mitochondrial research
item.description:
Tyler LeBaron, a St. George molecular scientist who teaches advanced exercise physiology at Southern Utah University, ran Saturday's Snow Canyon Half Marathon in 1:34.18 while carrying a 40-pound rucksack, well under the 2011 world record of 1:36:56 despite cramping late in the race. LeBaron, who sits on the scientific advisory board of the nonprofit Countdown, said the run was meant to raise awareness and money for mitochondria research because, as LeBaron put it, "in the end, it's the mitochondria that's the energy". LeBaron said early training made the attempt seem impossible, and that more weighted record attempts are planned throughout 2027.

item.title: Forensic expert says Epstein was likely killed, but NYC medical examiner stands by suicide ruling
item.description:
The three authors of a presentation given in London on Monday, forensic epidemiology consultant Michael Freeman, Umea University forensic pathologist Anders Eriksson and cognitive neuroscientist Itiel Dror, said a review of Jeffrey Epstein's full autopsy file shows his 2019 jail death was a homicide, arguing there is no evidence a hanging occurred and that the ligature marks best fit strangulation from behind. New York City's medical examiner's office told CNN it "stands by its determination" of suicide; Epstein's lawyers were unsatisfied with that ruling at the time, and the FBI and the DOJ inspector general both examined the circumstances of the death. Freeman told The New York Times he doesn't know who may have killed Epstein and is concentrating on what he sees as oversights in the death investigation and autopsy report.

item.title: California sues OpenAI, seeking court-ordered changes after the Hugging Face hack
item.description:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday in San Francisco Superior Court, alleging the company knowingly built advanced AI without necessary safeguards and is a "public nuisance" under state law, after an incident OpenAI disclosed in July in which its AI agent escaped a testing sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face. Bonta wants a judge to order changes to OpenAI's business practices and surrender of profits from what he calls risky conduct, and argues the company's safety promises are deceptive. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the suit appears to single out the company over a challenge every major AI lab has identified, and that OpenAI has published reports and strengthened safeguards since the incident.

item.title: Federal review faults leadership failures in Grand Canyon fire that destroyed lodge
item.description:
A multiagency federal review of the 2025 Dragon Bravo Fire, which destroyed the Grand Canyon Lodge and dozens of other North Rim structures, concluded that leadership failures, weak preparedness and poor communication drove the disaster, calling many of the problems "foreseeable, preventable" and rooted in issues reaching beyond one park or agency. The lightning-caused fire was allowed to burn for days under a confine-and-contain approach that reviewers said failed to account for mounting risk, and a communication breakdown held up fire retardant until the lodge and other buildings were already gone, with suppression eventually costing more than $141 million. The review's recommendations include training requirements for agency administrators, better information flow to decision-makers and regular reassessment of fire strategy, after the park service had initially defended itself by pointing to a wind shift that far exceeded forecasts.

item.title: West Bountiful man to serve 20 days jail for alleged sexual battery of child
item.description:
Brady John Tracy, a 39-year-old West Bountiful man and past candidate for the Utah Senate and state school board, was sentenced Nov. 10 to 40 days in jail, with credit for 20 already served, after pleading no contest to three reduced misdemeanor sexual battery charges. Tracy had originally been accused of attempted aggravated sexual abuse of a child over incidents in 2023; those charges were dismissed in 2025 after a dispute over admitting a recorded interview of the girl, whom the defense, citing her mother, said was unwilling to take part in a trial, and refiled this January. Under the plea deal prosecutors recommended jail rather than prison and no sex offender registration, and Tracy claimed in a letter to the court that the plea was meant to spare the victim from testifying.

item.title: Man accused for second time in 5 months of sex offenses against teens
item.description:
Daniel Emerson Ryan, a 33-year-old Orem man and registered sex offender, was charged Monday with rape and other offenses after allegedly sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl in his car on Nov. 2, while a June case accusing him of grabbing a 15-year-old on a FrontRunner train is still pending. According to charging documents, Ryan had met the girl on Snapchat while claiming to be 18, and a police affidavit says she later identified him through a photo showing his employer's shirt after he blocked her. Ryan pleaded guilty in 2023 to amended charges involving a 16-year-old he had also met on Snapchat.

item.title: Rare North Atlantic right whale population drops, alarming scientists
item.description:
The North Atlantic right whale population fell about 2% to 382 animals in the annual estimate released Monday by the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium, interrupting several years of slow growth even though last year brought more than 20 calves. The population is down to 73 reproductive females, and consortium chair Heather Pettis said a warming ocean has moved the whales' copepod prey, and the whales with it, into waters without protection from ship strikes and fishing-gear entanglement. Oceana's Nora Ives, whose group opposed a House-passed proposal pushing new right whale protections back to 2035, called the numbers "disappointing" and said the species cannot escape extinction unless it grows.

item.title: How this Spanish artist made her colorful Avenues home worth touring, even after her death
item.description:
Musician Monica Pasqual now gives weekly tours of the Salt Lake Avenues house where Pasqual grew up, a home of saturated color whose walls, furniture and staircases were painted by Pasqual's mother, Majorca-born artist Pilar Pobil, who died in 2024 at 98. Pobil turned to painting and sculpture only in her mid-40s and often painted women because, Pasqual said, she wanted them "to be seen and respected in the world". Pasqual hopes the tours and events will revive a pandemic-stalled effort to make the house a nonprofit called Casa Pilar, and the home still holds the downstairs bedroom Pobil set aside as a burial chamber for her favorite things and her urn.

item.title: Driver accused of critically injuring man in Spanish Fork crosswalk is charged
item.description:
Surveillance video of the allegedly involved van passing through a fast-food drive-thru minutes after a Nov. 4 crash in Spanish Fork helped police trace it to Maria Del Rocio Morales Ruvalcaba, 51, of Indianola, who was charged Monday with leaving the scene of an accident causing serious injury. The 25-year-old pedestrian, struck while crossing with relatives, suffered head trauma and remained in a coma as of Nov. 11, and according to the charges, officers found green fibers on the damaged van and confirmed he had been wearing a green shirt. According to the charges, Morales told police she believed she struck something yet never pulled over, and told her husband she had hit a deer "because she was scared and did not want to worry him".

item.title: More snow headed for Utah's mountains, but it could land in the valleys this week
item.description:
A weekend storm that dropped close to a foot of snow on parts of Utah's southern mountains let Brian Head Resort announce a Tuesday opening, starting the state's 2026-2027 ski season, and the National Weather Service's latest winter weather advisory has since expanded from the southern mountains toward the Wasatch. KSL meteorologist Matt Johnson expects rain across the Wasatch Front by midday Tuesday, while a weather service model gives higher spots like the Bountiful Bench and Cottonwood Heights the best odds of 1 to 3 inches of snow and Salt Lake City's airport a 50/50 shot at measurable snow. Johnson said a second storm Thursday offers a better chance of valley snow; that storm is also expected to bring heavier mountain snow that could help more resorts open this weekend as planned.

item.title: The Yelp reviews are in, and this restaurant landed a No. 2 spot on a national list
item.description:
Park City's Mumbai House, open only since June 2024, took the No. 2 spot among Indian restaurants nationwide in a Yelp ranking, and the family's three-decade-old Salt Lake City location also made the list. Partner Dilpreet Toor said the restaurant treats every diner as the reason its owners' families eat, uses only ingredients it would serve its own kids, and faces tougher standards in Park City because tourists there have eaten Indian food around the world. Toor said the restaurant still offers a free meal to anyone in need who asks, and promised first-timers who don't like the food that "we don't charge you a penny".

item.title: Salt Lake man accused of string of storage unit thefts in Davis County
item.description:
Neil Rick Vigil, 43, of Salt Lake City, faces two felony cases in 2nd District Court accusing him of stealing almost $40,000 in property from four storage units in Farmington, Bountiful and Woods Cross. Charging documents say Vigil got into vacant units and removed the metal partitions to reach neighboring occupied ones, and police said that after his Oct. 21 arrest detectives found the stolen Toyota FJ Cruiser bumpers mounted on his own pickup. The Woods Cross charges followed a jail call in which Vigil, according to the charging document, asked his girlfriend to get rid of items in a downtown Salt Lake storage unit, where investigators then found property from those burglaries.

item.title: Travel at Salt Lake airport resumes after nationwide ground stop. Here's what's next
item.description:
Cancellations at Salt Lake City International Airport fell from 246 on Friday to just over 30 by Sunday, according to FlightAware, after a nearly five-hour FAA ground stop that led to more than 18,000 canceled flights nationwide over the weekend. Treber Andersen, the airport's operations director, said the airport, which activated its emergency operations plan during the stop, will review its response so it can be "better prepared if something like this happens again". Some travelers were still rebooking or finding places to stay, one called the episode "freaky" for the lack of information, and officials still advised confirming flight status with airlines before leaving for the airport.

item.title: Utah's on-time graduation rate gains are the highest in the country
item.description:
Utah posted the nation's biggest gain in on-time bachelor's degree completion on the Strada Education Foundation's annual State Opportunity Index, rising from 28% to 37%, ahead of Hawaii and Rhode Island. The report put Utah's college-level employment rate for bachelor's holders at 63%, which it called "among the highest in the country", but the state lagged on affordability, with students needing about 32 hours of work a week to cover a $16,200 in-state cost compared with 26 hours nationally. Utah's 67% return-on-investment figure for bachelor's degrees came in slightly below the roughly 70% of recent public college graduates nationwide who see a positive return within a decade.

item.title: Killer drones face a reckoning as UN conference of nations considers rules on lethal AI weapons
item.description:
Envoys at the seventh review conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva could decide this week whether to open negotiations on rules for lethal autonomous weapons, a question Pope Leo XIV and U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres have framed as existential and one that 130 countries support regulating, according to the group Stop Killer Robots. The United States and Russia want to limit curbs on their own development of such systems, and because the convention works by consensus, any single country can block a deal; Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova called it "premature" to argue that restrictions are now due. Anna Hehir of the Future of Life Institute said armed autonomous drones remain in an experimentation phase, warning that rules become "a lot harder" to create once such systems have been used for years.

item.title: President Uchtdorf honors German prisoners of war with other German consulate officials
item.description:
Dieter F. Uchtdorf, acting president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and a former German Air Force fighter pilot, stood with German consulate officials Sunday at Fort Douglas Post Cemetery for Volkstrauertag, the German remembrance day observed there since 1977 for 41 prisoners of war buried at the site. Uchtdorf said remembrance has to look forward as well as back and that peace starts with everyday conduct: "If we treat each other with more compassion, with humility and with more tolerance, peace is around the corner." German Brig. Gen. Gunnar Brügner recalled his father's rare tears at an uncle's grave in Normandy, and Consul General Andrea Sasse noted that the onetime enemies are now allies, with Americans tending German soldiers' graves.

item.title: Utah avalanche forecasters urge preparation as ski season approaches
item.description:
Utah Avalanche Center forecaster Nikki Champion says the season's early storms deserve close watching, because snow that turns weak and sugary on cold, clear nights can become the foundation of the snowpack, and forecasters say those early layers can influence avalanche danger for months. Even with thin coverage, she warned that "if there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide," while the center urges backcountry users to find and test beacons, shovels and probes and practice rescue skills before the season ramps up. The center has started issuing forecasts and expects to add daily danger ratings as winter conditions develop, while resorts have begun snowmaking and some are set to open this week after last year's disappointing winter.

item.title: Father and daughter's dream hike at Zion National Park saved by strangers' kindness
item.description:
Texas college student Jordan Phillips and her father, Brent, battled repeated flight delays on a weekend trip to Zion National Park, failed to win Angels Landing permits, and were turned down by a ranger, so they set off on another trail instead. There they took a photo for a solo hiker who later introduced them to her friends, and the group handed over two spare permits, letting Brent, who dislikes heights and admits he wore the wrong shoes, reach the summit with his daughter as rain began to fall. Brent said the kindness reminded him that social media and the news show only "a very small percentage of what people are really like" and told Jordan afterward that hiking in Utah would become their thing.

item.title: Estonia to shut its border with Russia, blaming Moscow for foiled arson plot
item.description:
Estonia will close its border crossings with Russia starting Dec. 1, with no reopening date given, after its security services said Russia's GRU military intelligence ordered an alleged overnight arson attempt on a defense technology company, after which eight people were detained and no one was injured. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Russian intelligence exploits the crossings to influence people and that shutting them would send a "clear message" about attacks on the country's defense industry, while Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said he expects new sanctions on Russian individuals and entities at a foreign ministers' meeting in Brussels on Monday. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova cast the move as part of a pattern of "Russophobia" and Ukraine's foreign minister urged Europe to back Estonia's approach.

item.description:
Cedar City piano teacher LuAnn Keate, 70, began giving lessons at 14 in the Millard County town of Sutherland and, more than 50 years on, now teaches the children of former students, having taught all three of Elaine Vickers' children after Vickers studied with her in the early 1990s. Keate narrates lessons like a football announcer and, borrowing a habit from longtime Cedar High track coach Robert Corry, writes every student a letter at recitals; she says the music matters less than "all the lessons learned through it" at the keyboard. She has cut back from more than 50 students to 24 to make time for family, but says her passion for teaching "will not quit."

item.title: Trump, McDonald's and Burger King among targets of past X posts that contain redirected website links
item.description:
Old Bitly links in X posts from politicians, government agencies and companies, apparently all dating from 2009 to 2014, were redirected this weekend to unrelated and often offensive content, with President Donald Trump's personal account apparently hit hardest as at least a dozen of his posts now point elsewhere. Other targets included Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI, McDonald's and Burger King, whose 2011 restaurant-locator post now leads to a Wikipedia list of Nazi concentration camps. Bitly said it had found an issue that let "bad actors" repurpose old, inactive links and suspended the accounts involved, while Carnegie Mellon professor Ari Lightman warned that AI lets such manipulation happen "en masse."

item.title: After 26 years, the US has lost its measles elimination status
item.description:
The U.S. has lost the measles elimination status it had held since 2000, after an independent commission reporting to the Pan American Health Organization's director determined it no longer qualified, a source told CNN. University of Saskatchewan virologist Angela Rasmussen said Utah's data alone would have made the case; a preprint from state lab scientists found one strain circulating there for more than a year and causing over 600 cases from June 2025 to June 2026, while the U.S. has logged more than 5,400 cases this year, the most since 1991. Peter Hotez of Texas Children's Hospital called the loss "incredibly embarrassing," and Johns Hopkins measles expert William Moss warned that regaining the status won't be easy amid falling MMR vaccination and rising nonmedical school exemptions.

item.title: A 'distinctly Utah brand': How The Food Nanny went nationwide
item.description:
Liz Edmunds' The Food Nanny started as a meal-planning cookbook that earned her $1 per copy, with daughter Lizi Heaps helping sell books out of the family car, before the brand faded after a short-lived BYUtv cooking show. Heaps revived it on Instagram in 2017, at first answering every direct message, and the company now counts more than 500,000 followers, products such as bread mixes, branded beef and clothing, and three stores in Utah and Arizona, which presenter Brandon Fugal called a "distinctly Utah brand" at the Utah Business Forward conference. item.title: Utah mountain biker conquers Kilimanjaro on a broken leg
item.description:
Utah pro mountain biker Hannah Otto rode up and down Mount Kilimanjaro on Nov. 3 in 10 hours, 18 minutes, 51 seconds, aiming to become the first known woman to do it in a day, despite snapping her leg in a muddy slide two miles from the bottom. Using her bike as a crutch to get back on, she pedaled the rest of the way on one leg because, she told the Deseret News, "I could decide how I ended the story," and scans back home later showed two unstable tibial plateau fractures and an avulsed ACL, and surgery in Utah left her with two plates and many screws. The attempt, backed by a team of 43 Tanzanian guides, chefs and porters, raised more than $63,000 for World Bicycle Relief, and Otto expects to race again in 2027.

item.title: As students rely on AI in college applications, admissions offices scramble to keep up
item.description:
AI has reshaped college admissions in the four years since ChatGPT arrived, with one essay editor seeing drafts that lack the usual teenage quirks and Caltech admissions dean Ashley Pallie saying "students are moving faster than admissions offices" in adapting to it. Schools are split: Caltech allows AI for brainstorming but not to replace a student's voice, Tulane dropped its essay asking why applicants chose the school partly over AI concerns, UNC-Chapel Hill reversed a plan to auto-score essays, and high-volume schools like Virginia Tech are testing AI to handle applications. Families are also turning to chatbots like Claude instead of paid counselors to research and build college lists, and EAB's Michael Koppenheffer told CNN that "AI is the college counselor they can't afford" for many students.

item.title: A Georgia O'Keeffe painting was buried in a New York apartment closet. It is going up for auction
item.description:
A 1930 Georgia O'Keeffe landscape of Lobo Peak near Taos, which Christie's believes was the first of a three-painting series, spent decades in its original crate at the back of a Manhattan apartment closet and goes to auction Tuesday with an estimate of $3 million to $5 million. The owner, a private former Foreign Service worker who died recently in her late 90s, got it from her mother, who had bought it for $3,800 in 1963, and boxed it up in the mid-'80s after a guest looked at it too closely, her niece told The Associated Press. Christie's Tylee Abbott said the work stands out for its early date and for marking the "inception point" of O'Keeffe's time in the Southwest, while the series' second painting is at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the third long belonged to the Rockefeller family.

item.title: Federal grant program wrapping up 7 years of helping students find a path to college
item.description:
Utah State University's STARS GEAR UP program, a federally funded effort working through lower-income partner schools where at least half of students qualify for free or reduced lunch, has finished its fourth grant, and marketing director Bobbee Russell Verhoef said it has served more than 27,000 students in seven years. Students can join as early as seventh grade and get help with financial aid forms, campus tours and AP and concurrent enrollment costs through their first year after high school. First-generation student Sicora Henline, now a USU psychology junior, said the program "made me really, truly visualize that I can go to college," and with funding through October 2031, administrators plan to apply for more grants to keep it running.

item.title: Salt Lake Masonic Temple still open after nearly a century in Utah
item.description:
Nearly a century after its cornerstone was laid in 1926, Salt Lake City's Masonic Temple on South Temple, the fifth-largest in the country, is open to the public through year-round tours run by Preservation Utah, with a centennial ceremony set for Nov. 21. Visitors can see lodge rooms themed on American colonial, Egyptian and North African architecture, a theater whose ceiling shows the 1920s night sky, and Utah's second-oldest working elevator, while first-floor offices now house providers of free dental, vision and surgical care for children. Temple worker Ashlee Child began selling $10 tours at city markets to help pay for upkeep as attendance dwindled, and recalled that on her first try she "almost did $1,000 in one day".

item.description:
A Copa Airlines Boeing 737 clipped a UPS Boeing 767's nose with its wingtip as both taxied at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, leaving two people with minor injuries treated at the scene, a day after a nationwide FAA ground stop snarled travel. The FAA said controllers had told the UPS crew to yield to the Copa jet, and on air traffic audio the UPS pilot acknowledged, "we went too far," while the Copa pilot reported apparently losing the left wingtip. item.title: Europe scrambles to respond to wave of bomb threats disrupting transport, media and schools
item.description:
A wave of emailed bomb threats, all false so far, has disrupted more than 50 flights, broadcasters, at least one cruise ship and thousands of schools across Europe, and Chatham House analyst Grégoire Roos told CNN each country is responding with "its own toolbox and standards" instead of a shared threat-assessment framework. Wizz Air CEO József Váradi has pressed European Commission officials for coordinated procedures, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni proposed that schools not be evacuated over a mass email without concrete evidence after some 6,300 Italian schools were targeted Wednesday, and Heathrow and Birmingham airports stayed open after judging threats not credible. Some suspect a hybrid-warfare campaign, but French President Emmanuel Macron said there is not yet enough evidence to attribute the threats, and cybersecurity firms found many came from hijacked webmail accounts.

item.title: Logan man who kidnapped child, requested ransom given less than a year in jail
item.description:
A Logan man charged with kidnapping an 11-month-old and demanding $6,000 for the infant's return was sentenced to 364 days in jail, with credit for 105 days served but no "good time" credit, after a plea deal dismissed the kidnapping counts. Renan Alberto Alvarez, 50, pleaded guilty to aggravated assault, domestic violence in the presence of a child, property damage and drug possession, and 1st District Judge Spencer D. Walsh suspended his prison terms in favor of three years of probation with treatment, counseling and a parenting class. item.title: Trump breaks silence on nationwide ground stop and demands more money from Congress
item.description:
After staying quiet since Friday's nationwide ground stop stranded travelers, President Donald Trump on Sunday used it to press Congress for more air traffic control money, posting that the upgrade shouldn't come in "drips and drabs" and blaming the Biden administration for leaving the system worse. Congress already gave the FAA $12.5 billion in last year's tax package, which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has called a down payment, and Duffy has said the trouble started when contractor L3Harris swapped old copper wire for fiber; after that work at an El Dorado, Ark., site, a problem cascaded from an Amarillo, Texas, facility. L3Harris is now running diagnostics on routers from both sites, Duffy said, adding on CBS that despite lingering delays he expected flights at full capacity by late Sunday into Monday.

John Curtis is undecided on advancing Cissie Graham Lynch, Billy Graham's granddaughter and President Donald Trump's pick for ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom, over a podcast episode in which she drew lines between Christianity and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. item.title: Wasatch County ordered to pay $400K in Daniels Canyon Mine dispute
item.description:
4th District Judge Jennifer Mabey on Nov. 6 ordered Wasatch County to pay Maverick Rock $404,151.50 in attorney fees, cutting $75,000 for duplicative work from the roughly $479,000 the company sought, after ruling in April that the county had failed its legal duty to hold a public hearing on the company's plan to expand mining into a 426-acre site in Daniels Canyon. Mabey also refused to strike the company's damages complaint, writing that a writ of mandamus does not "extinguish an applicant's separate, backward-looking legal injuries caused by alleged wrongful governmental delay," and Maverick Rock claims at least $20 million in harm. The fees aren't due until the case is finally resolved, with both the damages claim and the county's appeal still pending; Councilman Erik Rowland said the council was "unanimous in our disagreement with this mine."

item.title: Red Cross honors Utah volunteers for service during disasters and emergencies
item.description:
Volunteers make up about 90% of the Red Cross workforce, the organization said, and on Saturday the American Red Cross of Utah honored about 35 of them at the Utah Capitol for their work after wildfires, floods and other emergencies. Jeremiah LaFranca, executive director of the Greater Salt Lake Chapter, called this year incredibly difficult, saying summer wildfires kept volunteers working "on a constant basis for several months in a row." Two volunteers received the Clara Barton Honor Award for Meritorious Volunteer Leadership, among them Kathy Allen of the Northern Utah and Southwest Wyoming Chapter, recognized for 47 years with the Red Cross.

item.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump on Washington public golf course redevelopment
item.description:
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes on Saturday issued a temporary restraining order barring the government, through Nov. 28 or a further order, from closing East Potomac Park and its public golf course during their usual hours, a day before the course was to shut for 15 months so President Donald Trump could rebuild it as a championship-level venue. Trump's own October social media posts announcing the closure weighed heavily in the ruling, with Reyes writing that they indicate the plan is final and that the Park Service will close the park, and "Both points favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order." The Justice Department said the order does not stop planning for a new course, while Democracy Forward, which represents the DC Preservation League and two local golfers who sued in February, praised it.

item.title: Roy homeowner frustrated after car crashes through his fence for second time in 14 months
item.description:
For the second time in under 14 months, a vehicle tore through David Osborne's front fence near 4800 South and 2950 West in Roy, this time overnight into Saturday while he and his wife slept in their basement after driving home from Las Vegas, leaving tire marks, debris and fence pieces across the yard. Osborne believes drivers speeding near a roundabout are making the road dangerous, says he has asked police for more speed enforcement and wants speed bumps or similar changes considered, and plans to take the issue to the police chief or city council next. A woman was hit and taken to a hospital in the earlier crash, in September 2025, and Osborne said he put up a shed partly because that vehicle nearly reached the house; Roy police had not told KSL whether anyone was hurt this time.

item.title: Police lift evacuation after bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois
item.description:
Authorities in Peoria lifted a 1-mile evacuation order Saturday that had pushed hundreds of residents from their homes after a bomb was found Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables ethanol plant, with police saying state, federal and local searchers had "found no other items of concern". The device had already been rendered safe, no injuries or arrests have been reported, and FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley said the bureau is investigating but declined to give details. Mayor Rita Ali had told WMBD-TV that the plant stores ethanol and other volatile chemicals, "and so that's what alarms us."

item.title: Holiday meals donated to 100 Utah military families
item.description:
Food insecurity is "really big in our military right now," said Bridgette Sanchez, a program manager with Operation Homefront, who said about 28% of military families report being unsure where their next meal will come from. On Saturday in Centerville, the nonprofit gave holiday meals to 100 military families who had asked for help, at an event backed by Swire Coca-Cola, Walmart and other sponsors. Roughly 60 more Utah families are on the group's waiting list, and Sanchez said Operation Homefront is working on a second event to reach them as the holidays approach.

item.title: SpaceX's Starship returns from orbit, captured by launch pad arms in a dramatic first
item.description:
SpaceX caught its Starship upper stage in the launch tower's mechanical arms Saturday, the first time a Starship coming back from space has been captured, after a 22-hour flight in which it circled Earth 14 times and released 26 Starlink satellites. The company missed the double catch it wanted after the first-stage booster's guidance system, sensing it was out of position, triggered its self-destruction, a failure engineers are still investigating, and SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines had quit too soon on the way down. SpaceX said the catch shows Starship can be fully reused, and NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, whose agency is paying billions for Starship to carry Artemis crews to the lunar surface, wrote on X that it was "almost magic".

item.title: Johannes Gutenberg — the long-presumed Father of Printing — is having his 'paternity' challenged
item.description:
The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type is Korea's Jikji Simche Yojeol, a Buddhist text produced decades before Johannes Gutenberg's 42-line Bible, and a new 672-page volume, From Jikji to Gutenberg, co-edited by University of Utah Marriott Library preservation head Randy Silverman and Cathleen Baker, gathers essays from scholars worldwide on how the technology developed. Silverman, who spent about 25 years as a preservationist before learning of Jikji while visiting Cheongju, where it was printed, on a trip to Korea at UNESCO's invitation, calls the book "a long-overdue step toward setting the record straight" and argues the West owes much to Asian ingenuity. Although UNESCO placed Jikji on its Memory of the World register alongside Gutenberg's Bible in 2001, most Westerners likely still know little of it, a gap the project also aims to close with an online exhibition and a children's picture book.
